To promote the use of indigenous vegetables like Okra that have play significant role in mitigate food insecurity and alleviate malnutrition in the country. However, Okra has been considered a minor crop and no attention was paid to its improvement in the international research program in past [20]. On the other hand, the demand for vegetable oils is rapidly increasing due to the growing human population and the expanding oil industry with health promoting oil components, the exploration of some underutilized and newer resources of vegetable oils is of much concern [21]. Okra, which is currently grown mainly as a vegetable crop, has potential for cultivation as an essential oilseed crop because okra seeds contain high amount of oil (20-40%) [22]. However, there is also no comprehensive literature information regarding characteristics of the oils produced from Okra seeds. Therefore, this review was aimed to assess literature regarding the nutritional quality and potential health benefits of edible parts of Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) vegetable. The oil compositions of okra seed was also discussed in order to provide further reliable information about health promoting oil components of Okra seeds. Nutritional composition of okra Okra is more a diet food than staple [23]. Okra seeds have been used on a small scale for oil production. Lipid components greatly contribute to the nutritional and sensory value of almost all types of foods. Nature provides a large number of fats that differ in their chemical and functional properties. Four classes of lipids are habitually found in vegetable oils: triacylglycerols, diacylglycerols, polar lipids, and free fatty acids. The fatty acid composition determines the physical properties, stability, and nutritional value of lipids. The most naturally occurring storage lipids are triacylglycerols. Triacylglycerols are natural compounds that consist of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids that differ in the length of their acyl chains and the number and positions of double bonds: saturated, monoenoic, and polyunsaturated fatty acids that differ with respect to detailed fatty acid composition. Monoenoic fatty acids and polyunsaturated fatty acids are structurally distinguished by the presence of repeating methylene units. These units produce an extremely flexible chain that rapidly reorients through conformational states and constitutes an influential group of molecules that promote health [24]. Okra seeds from Greece are a potential source of oil, with concentrations varying from 20% to 40%, depending on the extraction method. The oil mainly consists of linoleic acid (up to 47.4%). Okra seed oil is a rich source of linoleic acid, a polyunsaturated fatty acid essential for human nutrition [25]. Proteins play a particularly important role in human nutrition. The amino acid contents, proportions, and their digestibility by humans characterize a protein’s biological value [26]. Okra has been called “a perfect villager’s vegetable” because of its robust nature, dietary fiber, and distinct seed protein balance of both lysine and tryptophan amino acids (unlike the proteins of cereals and pulses) [27]. The amino acid composition of okra seed protein is comparable to that of soybean and the PER is higher than that of soybean [28] and the amino acid pattern of the protein renders it an adequate supplement to legume or cereal based diets [29]. Okra seed is known to be rich in high quality protein especially with regards to its content of essential amino acids relative to other plant protein sources. Hence, it plays a vital role in the human diet [30]. Okra also contains carbohydrates and vitamins [31-33], and plays a vital role in human diet [34]. Consumption of young immature okra pods is important as fresh fruits, and it can be consumed in different forms. Fruits can be boiled, fried or cooked [35]. The composition of okra pods per 100 g edible portion (81% of the product as purchased, ends trimmed) is: water 88.6 g, energy 144.00 kJ (36 kcal), protein 2.10 g, carbohydrate 8.20 g, fat 0.20 g, fibre 1.70 g, Ca 84.00 mg, P 90.00 mg, Fe 1.20 mg, β-carotene 185.00 μg, riboflavin 0.08 mg, thiamin 0.04 mg, niacin 0.60 mg, ascorbic acid 47.00 mg. The composition of okra leaves per 100 g edible portion is: water 81.50 g, energy 235.00 kJ (56.00 kcal), protein 4.40 g, fat 0.60 g, carbohydrate 11.30 g, fiber 2.10 g, Ca 532.00 mg, P 70.00 mg, Fe 0.70 mg, ascorbic acid 59.00 mg, β-carotene 385.00 μg, thiamin 0.25 mg, riboflavin 2.80 mg, niacin 0.20 mg [36]. Carbohydrates are mainly present in the form of mucilage [37,38]. That of young fruits consists of long chain molecules with a molecular weight of about 170,000 made up of sugar units and amino acids. The main components are galactose (25%), rhamnose (22%), galacturonic acid (27%) and amino acids (11%). The mucilage is highly soluble in water. Its solution in water has an intrinsic viscosity value of about 30%. Potassium, Sodium, Magnesium and Calcium are the principal elements in pods, which contain about 17% seeds. Presence of Iron, Zink, Manganese and Nickel also has been reported [39]. Fresh pods are low in calories (20 per 100 g), practically no fat, high in fiber, and have several valuable nutrients, including about 30% of the recommended levels of vitamin C (16 to 29 mg), 10 to 20% of folate (46 to 88 mg) and about 5% of vitamin A (14 to 20 RAE). Both pod skin (mesocarp) and seeds are excellent source of zinc (80 mg/g) [40]. Okra seed is mainly composed of oligomeric catechins (2.5 mg/g of seeds) and flavonol derivatives (3.4 mg/g of seeds), while the mesocarp is mainly composed of hydroxycinnamic and quercetin derivatives (0.2 and 0.3 mg/g of skins). Pods and seeds are rich in phenolic compounds with important biological properties like quartering derivatives, catechin oligomers and hydroxycinnamic derivatives. These properties, along with the high content of carbohydrates, proteins, glycol-protein, and other dietary elements enhance the importance of this foodstuff in the human diet [41]. Dried okra sauce (pods mixed with other ingredients and regularly consumed in West Africa) does not provide any beta carotene (vitamin A) or retinol [42]. However, fresh okra pods are the most important vegetable source of viscous fiber, an important dietary component to lower cholesterol [43]. Seven-days-old fresh okra pods have the highest concentration of nutrients [44]. Seed as potential edible oil and flour source Okra seeds contain about 20 to 40% oil. The bark fibre is easy to extract. It is white to yellow in colour, strong but rather coarse. Tests conducted in China suggest that an alcohol extract of okra leaves can eliminate oxygen free radicals, alleviate renal tubular-interstitial diseases, reduce proteinuria, and improve renal function. Okra seed can be dried, and the dried seeds are a nutritious material that can be used to prepare vegetable curds, or roasted and ground to be used as coffee additive or substitute [45]. Okra seed oil yield is comparable to most oil seed crops except oil palm and soybean. Moreover, okra seed oil has potential hypocholesterolemic effect. The potential for wide cultivation of okra for edible oil as well as for cake is very high. Okra seed flour could also be used to fortify cereal flour [46]. For example, supplementing maize ogi with okra meal increases protein, ash, oil and fiber content [47]. Okra seed flour has been used to supplement corn flour for a very long time in countries like Egypt to make better quality dough. Mucilage and its potential Okra mucilage refers to the thick and slimy substance found in fresh as well as dried pods. Mucilaginous substances are usually concentrated in the pod walls and are chemically acidic polysaccharides associated with proteins and minerals [56]. Although nature of the polysaccharides varies greatly, neutral sugars rhamnose, galactose and galacturonic acid have been reported often. The okra mucilage can be extracted as a viscous gum using various procedures. Such diversity in the extraction procedures seems to contribute to the observed variability in the mucilage chemical composition [57]. Okra mucilage is a renewable and inexpensive source of biodegradable material. Its physical and chemical properties include high water solubility, plasticity, elasticity and viscosity [58]. Most physical and chemical properties are influenced by factors such as temperature, pH, sugar and salt contents, and storage time [59]. Okra mucilage has potential for use as food, non-food products, and medicine. Food applications include use as a whipping agent for reconstituted egg whites, as an additive in the formulation of flour-based adhesives, and as an additive in India for clarifying sugarcane juice. Non-food applications include brightening agents in electro deposition of metals, as a deflocculant in paper and fabric production, and as a protectant to reduce friction in pipe-flow. Polysaccharides can be combined with acrylamide to develop new biodegradable polymeric materials [60]. Potential of mucilage for medicinal applications includes uses as an extender of serum albumin, as tablet binder [61] and as suspending agent in formulations. Okra mucilage is used in Asian medicine as a protective food additive against irritating and inflammatory gastric diseases [62]. Health benefits of okra In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to the role of diet in human health [63]. The high intake of plant products is associated with a reduced risk of a number of chronic diseases, such as atherosclerosis and cancer [64]. These beneficial effects have been partly attributed to the compounds which possess antioxidant activity. The major antioxidants of vegetables are vitamins C and E, carotenoids, and phenolic compounds, especially flavonoids. These antioxidants scavenge radicals and inhibit the chain initiation or break the chain propagation (the second defense line). Vitamin E and carotenoids also contribute to the first defense line against oxidative stress, because they quench singlet oxygen [65]. Flavonoids as well as vitamin C showed a protective activity to α-atocopherol in human LDL, and they can also regenerate vitamin E, from the α-chromanoxy radical [66]. Nutrient antioxidants may act together to reduce reactive oxygen spieces level more effectively than single dietary antioxidants, because they can function as synergists [67]. In addition, a mixture containing both water-soluble and lipid-soluble antioxidants is capable of quenching free radicals in both aqueous and lipid phases [68]. For example, with the liposome oxidation method, the activity of combination of quercetin or catechins plus α-tocopherol was significantly higher than the sum of the individual activities. Combinations of α-tocopherol or vitamin C plus phenolic compounds also provided synergistic effects in human erythrocyte membrane ghosts and phosphatidylcholine liposome systems [69]. Okra seed is rich in protein and unsaturated fatty acids such as linoleic acid. In some countries, okra also is used in folk medicine as antiulcerogenic, gastroprotective, diuretic agents [70]. However, little information on antioxidant capabilities of major phenolic compounds from okra seed is available. Okra is also a popular health food due to its high fiber, vitamin C, and folate content. Okra is also a good source of calcium and potassium. Okra pod contains thick slimy polysaccharides, which are used to thicken soups and stews, as an egg white substitute, and as a fat substitute in chocolate bar cookies and in chocolate frozen dairy dessert. Okra is also known for being high in antioxidants activity with different parts of the plant [71,72] Atawodi has reported in vitro antioxidant assay of methanol extract of okra fruits. They have done antioxidant/radical scavenging activities by xanthine oxidase and 2-deoxyguanosine methods and reported 50% inhibitory concentration values of 25 and 43 ml. In addition, Arapitsas reported that Okra seed is rich in Phenolic compounds, mainly composed of flavonol derivatives and oligomeric catechins. According to Khomsug [73] total phenolic content of pulped and seeds of okra extracts as 10.75 ± 0.02 mg GAE/100g extract and 142.48 ± 0.02 mg GAE/100g extract which corresponds with scavenging activities. Besides they have also found procycanidin B2 as predominant phenolic compound followed by procycanidin B1 and rutin in seeds. In pulped seed catechin, procycanidin B2, epicatechin and rutin are reported to be present. It is quite important to the see that roasting (1600°C for 10-60 minutes) increased the nutrient composition and antioxidant activity of the seeds whereas pre-treatment (soaking and blanching) increased the nutrient composition, but decreases antioxidant activity [74,75]. Ansari reported Okra extract as in vitronon-enzymatic inhibitior of lipid peroxidation in liposomes. A. esculentus peel and seed powder contains significant in vivo antioxidant property in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats. Administration of different doses of peel and seed powder significantly increased liver, kidney and pancreas superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, reduced glutathione levels and decreased thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) (P<0.001) levels in diabetic rats compared to diabetic control rats [76]. Liao has done a comparative analysis of total phenolics and total flavonoids and antioxidant ability of different organs (flower, fruit, leaf, and seed) and different enrichment fractions of water extracts of the A. esculentus plant. They confirmed fruitful presence of total phenolics and total flavonoids related to antioxidant ability in all the extracts of the plant organs although percentage varied. In flower of okra highest amount of total phenolics and totalflavonoids were found. This data suggests Okra as a good contributor to the antioxidant status and promising chemopreventive agent as described in several traditional medicines for human race. Okra is abundant with several vitamins, minerals, and nutrients that handles the health advantages the plant provides. Here are a few of okra’s health advantages: • Okra contain high fiber, which “helps to stabilize blood sugar by regulating the rate at which sugar is absorbed from the intestinal tract”. Because of fiber along with other nutrition, okra shows useful for minimizing blood sugar levels within the body, assisting along with diabetes. The fiber likewise helps support blood sugar levels level simply by slowing down sugar assimilation through the intestines [77]. The frequent usage of okra might help avoid kidney disease. Within the research, “those who consumed okra every day decreased clinical indications of kidney damage a lot more than the ones that simply consumed a diabetic diet.” This ties along with diabetes, as almost 50% of kidney disease cases are generated by diabetes [78].

One hundred grams of okra also contain approximately 27 percent of our RDI of vitamin C and 50 percent of our RDI of vitamin K. Vitamin C is, of course, an essential antioxidant that aids in the growth and repair of bodily tissues. For this reason, eating more okra can rejuvenate our skin and hair, and also shield us from degenerative diseases associated with long-term free radical damage. Vitamin K, on the other hand, plays an important role in blood clot formation. If you suffer from regular nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavy menstrual bleeding, or easy bruising, your blood might be too thin. Consider adding more vitamin K-rich foods like okra to your diet to improve your blood’s ability to coagulate [81]. • Okra is used to promotes a healthy of the pregnancy. An incredibly essential B vitamin for creating and maintaining new cells, foliate is a vital substance for optimum pregnancy. The vitamin aids in preventing birth defects just like spina bifida and enables the baby to develop completely. Vitamin C is additionally required for baby development. Okra is full of both foliate and vitamin C. The high quantity of foliate included in the okra is helpful for the fetus while pregnant. Foliate is a vital nutrient that increases the growth and development of the fetus’ brain. The high quantity of folic acid within okra performs a huge role within the neural tube formation of the fetus through the fourth to the 12th week of pregnancy [82]. • Okra is used to improves heart health. The soluble fiber within okra helps you to reduce serum cholesterol and therefore decreases the chance of cardiovascular disease. Consuming okra is an efficient method to manage the body’s cholesterol level. Okra is additionally loaded with pectin that can help in reducing high blood cholesterol simply by modifying the creation of bile within the intestines. Okra is also used to improves good eyesight. The okra pods are fantastic options for Vitamin A and also beta carotene that are both important nourishment for sustaining an excellent eye-sight along with healthy skin. Additionally, these types of important nourishment also assist inhibits eye associated illnesses along with problems on the skin. Okra is better ingested when joined along with other healthy veggies. Consuming okra has truly numerous advantages, simply bear in mind to eat natural veggies as opposed to processed veggies. • Okra is used to controls the body’s cholesterol level. There are numerous significant illnesses related to high cholesterol level of the entire body. Managing the body’s cholesterol level is nearly difficult because it’s hard to avoid foods loaded with cholesterol content. One of the better health advantages of consuming okra is definitely the powerful management of the human body’s high cholesterol level. This healthy vegetable is beneficial in slimming down and also decreasing cholesterol therefore keeps a healthy and also low cholesterol body. Okra have been taken advantage by diet advisors due to these qualities. • Generally, okra is used to stabilize blood sugar by regulating the rate at which sugar is absorbed from the intestinal tract. It is a good vegetable for those feeling weak, exhausted, and suffering from depression and it is also used in ulcers, lung inflammation, sore throat as well as irritable bowel. Okra is good for asthma patients and it also normalizes blood sugar and cholesterol levels. Previous studies reported that okra polysaccharide possesses anticomplementary and hypoglycemic activity in normal mice [83]. Also, okra polysaccharide lowers cholesterol level in blood and may prevent cancer by its ability to bind bile acids. Additionally, Okra seed possess blood glucose normalization and lipid profiles lowering action in diabetic condition [84]. Conclusion The information presented here shows the potential nutritional importance of Okra and its role in improved nutrition and health. It is an affordable source of protein, carbohydrates, minerals and vitamins, dietary fibre and health promoting fatty acids. Scientific studies provide some evidence to support the potential beneficial effects of Okra components in lowering the risk for various chronic diseases, although information pertaining to the role of edible plant parts of Okra in disease prevention and the mechanisms of action are limited to date. This is due to the complex nature of disease etiology and various factors impacting their occurrence. It is imperative the scientific community continues to unravel the mechanisms involved in disease prevention and determine how food bio-actives from such foods as Okra can influence human health. Further research, needs to be performed to provide compelling evidence for the direct health benefits of Okra consumption. Therefore, promoting the consumption of traditional vegetables such as Okra could provide cheap sources of macro and micronutrients and mineral elements that can improve the nutritional status of resource-poor subsistence farmers in the area in particular and in Ethiopia in general. Furthermore, this vegetable can also be used as an indispensable tool when it comes to reducing the prevalence of malnutrition, especially among resource-constrained urban households in addition to rural household. Consumption of Okra by both low-income and high-income groups can also used as a means of dietary diversification approach. References 1. 852 Indian Journal of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, January-March 2021, Vol. 15, No. 1 A Mini-Review of the Medicinal Properties of Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus L.) and Potential Benefit against SARS-CoV-2 Arif Nur Muhammad Ansori Doctoral Student, Doctoral Program in Veterinary Science, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya, Indonesia. Abstract Indonesia is rich in medicinal plants, where its population has traditionally used them for generations to cure diseases. Traditional medicine and medicinal plants from Indonesia may lead to the discovery of novel drugs. Abelmoschus esculentus L. or okra is well known as a cure for several diseases and is included in various folk medicinal stockpiles. In recent decades, scientists have discovered the phytochemical composition in the whole okra plant, as well as its pharmacological activities. These studies established the therapeutic potential of okra for drug discovery. Therefore, the present review provides a sneak peek of okra’s pharmacology and phytochemistry, also the potential benefit against SARS-CoV-2. Keywords: Abelmoschus esculentus L., medicinal properties, SARS-CoV-2. Corresponding author: Arif Nur Muhammad Ansori Email: arif.nma-17@fkh.unair.ac.id Introduction Indonesia is encompassed by many vegetations, including tropical rain forests. Additionally, Indonesia is one of the top five countries in the world that has a high plant diversity, including approximately 6,000 medicinal plants1. Consequently, Indonesia is rich in medicinal plants that is used by its population to cure many diseases2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. One of the medicinal plants in Indonesia is Abelmoschus esculentus L. or okra. Okra is also called qiu kui, bendi, lady’s finger, gumbo, dharos, kacang, and bamieh. It is usually cultivated in warm temperate and tropical regions worldwide and belongs to the Malvaceae family10. Okra is a medicinal plant due to the multiple benefits of its seeds, buds, stems, flowers, leaves, and pods in traditional and contemporary medicine11. Okra fruits traditionally have been used as aphrodisiac, appetizer, cooling, and astringent agents. Other uses of okra include treatment of gonorrhea, bladder blockage, urinary discharges, diarrhea, and chronic dysentery. Okra seeds have also been used as fungicide agents, anti-tumor, and anti-cancer12. The pharmacological properties of okra, such as antioxidant13, anti-inflammatory14, immunomodulatory15, gastroprotective14, neuroprotective16, lipid-lowering17, anti-cancer18, antibacterial18, and anti-diabetic properties19 (Figure 1). Therefore, the present review provides a sneak peek view into okra’s pharmacology and phytochemistry against SARS-CoV-2. Okra Distribution The okra plant grows annually up to 1 m. The plant prefers light (sandy), requires clay soils and welldrained moist soil. The plant prefers basic (alkaline), neutral, acidic soils, and it can grow in very alkaline soil. This plant cannot grow in the shade. The flowers are pollinated by bees and insects and are hermaphrodite (with both male and female organs). The flowers of the okra plant bloom approximately from June to October10. Chemical Composition The main components of okra bast fiber are lignin, hemicellulose, α-cellulose, and the rest are minor in

Indian Journal of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, January-March 2021, Vol. 15, No. 1 853 proportion10. The chemical contexture of okra bast fibers, such as 2.7% aqueous extract, 3.9% fatty and waxy matter, 3.4% pectin matter, 7.1% lignin, 15.4% hemicellulose, and 67.5% α-cellulose2,4,5,8. Nutritional Potential of Okra Ca, Mg, Na, and K are the important elements in okra pods, which contain approximately 17% seeds; the presence of Ni, Mn, Zn, and Fe has also been reported20. A fresh okra pods are low in calories, no fat, high in fiber, and many precious nutrients, including approximately 10-20% folate (46-88 g), about 5% of vitamin A, approximately 30% of the recommended levels of vitamin C (16-29 mg), and both okra mesocarp and seeds are good sources of zinc (80 g/g)21, 22. Flavonol derivatives (3.4 mg/g of seeds) and oligomeric catechins (2.5 mg/g of seeds) are importantly composed of okra seeds. On the other hand, the mesocarp is structured of quercetin derivatives and hydroxycinnamic acid, 0.3 and 0.2 mg/g of skins, respectively. Seeds and pods are composed in phenolic compounds with notable biological properties such as hydroxycinnamic derivatives, catechin oligomers, and quercetin derivatives23. These components, along with the high content of glycoproteins, proteins, carbohydrates, and other dietary elements, enhance the importance in the human diet24,23. On the other hand, a dried okra sauce does not provide any vitamin A or retinol25. However, fresh okra pods, an important dietary component to lower cholesterol, are the most notable vegetable source of fiber. In addition, seven-day-old fresh okra pods have the highest concentration of nutrients26. Okra’s Benefits for Human Health Okra is useful for minimizing blood sugar levels, and therefore beneficial in diabetes, owing to the fiber content, along with other nutritional components. Okra contains high fiber and helps to stabilize blood sugar levels by regulating the rate at which sugar is absorbed. Previous studies have reported that okra polysaccharide possesses hypoglycemic activity and anti-complementary in normal mice8. Additionally, okra can be used in kidney disease prevention17. The okra pods are high in beta-carotene and vitamin A, which are important for healthy skin and sustaining eyesight. Okra is used to rectify eyesight. Additionally, these types of nutrients also assist in inhibiting skin related problems and eye-associated diseases26. The soluble fiber within okra helps to reduce serum cholesterol. Okra is also loaded with pectin, which can help in reducing high blood cholesterol. Consuming okra is an efficient method for managing the body’s cholesterol level. Okra used to improve heart health27. Okra is a good vegetable for those exhausted and feeling weak. Okra is also used in asthma, irritable bowel lung inflammation, ulcers, and sore throat26. Okra used to treat many digestive system problems. Okra is used to support colon health. The polysaccharides present in okra pods suggested that they help to erase the adhesive between stomach tissue and bacteria, preventing bacteremia. Okra’s polysaccharides are effective at inhibiting the adhesion of Helicobacter pylori. Therefore, okra can create an environment that prevents destructive cultures from flourishing and cleanse our stomach. Okra smoothly moves down the colon, excess water in its path and absorbing toxins27. Mucilage are very rich in okra roots and have a sturdily demulcent action. This mucilage can be used as a plasma replacement. The roots infusion is used in the medication of syphilis. In Nepal, the juice of the roots is used to treat boils, wounds, and cuts. In addition, the leaves furnish an emollient poultice. Then, a decoction of the immature capsules is used as diuretic, emollient, and demulcent. It is used in the medication of dysuria, gonorrhea, and catarrhal infections. The seeds of okra have stimulant properties and anti-spasmodic. On the other hand, infusion of the okra roasted seeds also has specific properties10. Based on these numerous beneficial properties, okra may be a viable candidate against the SARS-CoV-2, but we need many confirmatory studies such as in silico, in vitro, and in vivo (Figure 1).

ABSTRACT

Abelmoschus esculentus (L.) Moench is also called as okra or lady's finger and is an important food and medicinal plant which is widely used in tropical and sub-tropical countries. In addition to its nutritional benefits, the plant also has a variety of bioactive compounds, including flavonoids, phenolic acids, polysaccharides, mucilage, phytosterols, tannins, carotenoids, and other secondary metabolites. The current review compiles the botanical features, ethnomedicinal significance, nutritional profile, phytochemical composition, pharmacological activity and molecular mechanisms of A. esculentus. Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antihyperlipidemic, anti-obesity, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, nephroprotective, gastroprotective, antimicrobial, anticancer, neuroprotective, immunomodulatory, and wound-healing properties have been suggested in the preclinical studies. The effects seem to be multifaceted and involve a variety of interconnected mechanisms such as regulation of oxidative stress, NF-κB-mediated inflammation, inflammatory cytokines, insulin signalling, AMPK-associated metabolic pathways, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and gut microbiota-related mechanisms. Gastrointestinal protection, metabolic regulation and the potential prebiotic effect are other roles of polysaccharides and mucilage. Though there are some encouraging experimental results, clinical translation is hampered by plant variability in extraction, phytochemical content, dosing, and a lack of pharmacokinetic and human studies. Standardized extracts, identification of marker compounds, mechanistic validation, bioavailability studies, safety studies and clinical trials, should therefore be the focus of future investigations. In conclusion, A. esculentus is a promising functional food and phytopharmacological source that can be utilized in the development of nutraceuticals and therapeutic agents.

Keywords- Abelmoschus esculentus; okra; phytoconstituents; pharmacological activity; polysaccharides; flavonoids; antioxidant; antidiabetic; signalling pathways; nutraceuticals.

1.2 Historical and traditional medicinal relevance A. esculentus can be used for more than a vegetable. Various parts of the plant have been used in traditional and folk medicine for a long time in different parts of Africa and Asia. Uses include digestive disorders, inflammation, urinary disorders, weakness, respiratory disorders and metabolic disorders. The mucilaginous properties of the pods have been especially responsible for their traditional applications in irritation of the gastrointestinal tract. The mucilage of okra has been more or less considered as a soothing and protective substance due to its viscous and demulcent nature. Pods or roots have been used to prepare something that calms down the stomach and makes it comfortable. The plant has been used in traditional medicine for its alleged hypoglycemic properties as well, indicating an early understanding of its potential metabolic effects. Some communities have used seeds, as nutritional supplements, and seed extracts as traditional medicines; leaves and flowers have also been utilized in traditional health care [3]. Historically, okra has been used as a food and medicine due to its medicinal properties. Long term dietary exposure may give an indication of both the safety and therapeutic value of such plants which are of particular importance in ethnopharmacology. Experimental explanations have now started to be given for some of these traditional applications. For instance, the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of okra extracts could be the reasons for its traditional applications in inflammatory conditions, whereas the soluble dietary fibre, polysaccharides, and polyphenols may be responsible for the reported role in glucose and lipid metabolism. The composition and biological activity of plant preparations can vary significantly with cultivar, geographic origin, plant part, maturity, extraction method and processing conditions. Thus, traditional knowledge needs to be combined with phytochemical characterization, pharmacological validation, toxicological evaluation, and adequately-designed clinical studies [4]. 1.3 Nutritional and therapeutic importance One of the important nutritional reasons of the widespread dietary importance of A. esculentus is its nutritional value. Fresh pods are a source of dietary fibre, carbohydrates, small amounts of protein and fat and a few micronutrients. They are especially useful for their vitamin, mineral and bioactive plant compounds. Okra is also rich in folate, vitamin C, carotenoids, calcium, potassium, magnesium, and other nutritionally important components. The seeds have relatively higher protein and lipid content and may be used as a potential source of nutritional food. Okra also has a lot of mucilage which is a distinguishing feature of okra. The primary constituent of this mucilage was found to be complex polysaccharide, which gives the cooked pods their characteristic viscosity. Soluble fibre and mucilaginous polysaccharides could have a physiological effect on slowing gastrointestinal transit and perhaps both glucose and lipid absorption. The properties have led to studies on the use of okra in controlling diabetes, lowering cholesterol, supporting digestive health, and promoting weight loss [5]. Therapeutic potential of A. esculentus is highly related to synergistic effect of its phytochemicals, which includes no single individual. II. BOTANICAL PROFILE OF ABELMOSCHUS ESCULENTUS

Abelmoschus esculentus (L.) an important vegetable and medicinal plant of the family Malvaceae, Moench commonly known as okra, lady's finger, bhindi or gumbo. An annual herbaceous warm season crop that is grown widely in tropical and subtropical areas. It is mainly used for the immature edible pods as well as for the leaves, flowers, seeds, roots and mucilage which are also edible and medicinal. There is a high degree of variation in the botanical traits of A. esculentus between cultivars, especially plant height, pod shape, colour, pubescence, flowering and maturity period. Abelmoschus esculentus is part of the Kingdom Plantae, Order Malvales, Family Malvaceae, Genus Abelmoschus and species A. esculentus. The species was formerly classified in the genus Hibiscus and so the species name Hibiscus esculentus L. was used, but since then new classification has been based on morphological and reproductive traits, and thus Abelmoschus is a new genus. Scientific name: Abelmoschus esculentus (L.), is the value used globally. Presently, its use is widespread in botanical, agricultural and pharmacological literature. The plant reaches a height of about 1-2 m, and may reach much greater heights if growing conditions are ideal. Stem erect, stout, cylindrical, often with both fine and coarse hairs. Depending on the cultivar, branching may be limited or extensive. The root system is composed mostly of a strong taproot with many lateral roots that allow the plant to access water and nutrients from the deeper soil layers. It also helps it to adapt to warm conditions, but can be detrimental under drought conditions, particularly in terms of yield and pod quality [7]. Leaves are alternate and on long petioles. The leaves are broad, palmately lobed, and typically with 3-7 lobes with serrated edges. Lobing and leaf size are dependent on the cultivar, stage of growth and environmental conditions. The leaves are typically green with more or less indumentary. Besides their photosynthetic function, okra leaves are also eaten as vegetables in some parts of the world and studied for their phytochemical and pharmacological properties. A. esculentus flowers are big, showy, hermaphroditic and usually solitary in the axils of the leaves. They are similar to those of other members of Malvaceae. Corolla is typically 5 pale yellow or cream-colored petals with a distinct dark reddish or purplish centre of the corolla near its base. The stamens are fused into a staminal column and the ovary is superior and multilocular. Okra is self pollinated with some cross pollination occurring by insect pollination, primarily by bees [9]. After flowering, the fruit is an elongated capsule-like structure that grows quickly. Pods can be green, light green, dark green, reddish or even purple, depending on genotype. They can be cylindrical and smooth, ridged and angular. Immature pods are tender, have mucilage and are generally collected within a couple days post flowering for culinary purposes. As the fruit ripens, the flesh becomes fibrous, and the seeds become numerous and round and are enclosed in longitudinal compartments. Typically they are kidney-shaped, greyish green to dark brown when mature, and are spherical. They are rich in protein, carbohydrates, oil, minerals and bioactives. Okra is grown throughout India, Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and in parts of the Americas. It thrives best in warm climates, generally in fertile, welldrained soils in a good amount of sunlight. The plant is frost- and cold-sensitive, and requires warm climates to thrive well. Due to its wide geographical distribution, morphological variability and adaptability, A. esculentus has developed many cultivars, which differ in yield, pod morphology, nutritional composition, and phytochemical content. This plant and genetic variability is especially important in developing medicine as the levels of the pharmacologically active constituents can vary from plant variety to plant variety, and from plant part to plant part. Thus, botanical identification, documentation of cultivar and selection of the appropriate plant material is vital for repeatable phytochemical and pharmacological studies [10].

Abelmoschus esculentus is a plant with a long history of food-crop utilization and as a traditional medicinal plant. It is the most widely cultivated species in Asia, Africa, Middle East and other tropical and subtropical areas, and consequently has many ethnobotanical applications. The leaves, flowers, roots, immature pods and seeds have been employed in traditional medicine and home remedies. These applications are closely linked with the mucilage, dietary fibre, polyphenols, flavonoids, vitamins, minerals, etc. which are also present in the plant. Many of these

The immature pods of A. esculentus are most commonly used. They are eaten in traditional diets as vegetables in boiled, fried, stewed and dried format. They are used as a gastrointestinal tonic with a high mucilage content in gastrointestinal diseases as well. In a few traditional remedies, okra preparations have been used for the management of gastric irritation and constipation and to soothe the stomach discomfort. The mucilaginous polysaccharides in the pods are thought to have demulcent properties through a protective film on irritated mucous membranes. This is a traditional use, consistent with current interest in the gastroprotective and digestivehealth properties of okra [11]. Traditionally, okra is also known to be useful for diabetes and other metabolic disturbances. Pods in some community are cut into slivers and put into water to make a mucilaginous liquid that is taken as a remedy at home to reduce high blood glucose. Pod extracts are also used in traditional remedies for metabolic health, as are seed extracts. These practices have encouraged experimental research to elucidate the antihyperglycemic, insulin sensitizing and lipid-lowering effects of A. esculentus. Polyphenolic compounds, soluble fibre and polysaccharides have been suggested as key compounds to play a role in these effects due to their potential to modulate intestinal glucose transport, carbohydrate metabolism, oxidative stress, and metabolic signalling. The roots and leaves of A. esculentus have also been used for folk medicine. Leaves used for food; or as decoctions and poultices. They have been traditionally used for inflammatory conditions, as a treatment for pain and for skin complaints. Leaves have been crushed and used externally for wounds, boils and itchy skin at times. These practices are of interest in the field of pharmacology as okra leaves are rich in phenolic compounds and other components that have been documented for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties [12]. Pods are not as commonly used as roots but are important in some ethnomedicinal systems. Root decoction and mucilaginous preparations were traditional medicines used as demulcents and for gastrointestinal and urinary irritation. In certain areas, preparations have also been used for respiratory discomfort, and inflammatory complaints. The roots have been investigated less than the fruits and seeds and therefore there is a need to investigate the root phytochemical composition and pharmaceutical activity. Okra seeds have nutritional and ethnobotanical values. The matured seeds are rich in protein, oil, minerals and polyphenolic compounds, and can be roasted or ground or used in food preparations. In some traditional settings, roasted seeds have been used as a coffee substitute. Preparations made from seeds have also been linked to tonic and nutritional purposes. Some traditional uses of seeds may have a scientific background for their antioxidant, antihyperlipidemic, and metabolic regulatory properties, as evidenced by the current research. A. esculentus flowers are less used, but also used in traditional preparations in some localities. They have flavonoids and phenolic compounds, which could be involved in antioxidant activity, like other parts of the plant. Multiple use of plant parts shows that the ethnobotanical value of okra is not limited to its edible pods [13]. In conclusion, the historical medicinal applications of A. esculentus offer valuable insights into its potential for modern pharmacological research. Experimental research indicates that there are several ethnomedicinal claims that are supported, such as gastrointestinal protection, glucose regulation, inflammation, and oxidative stress. However, there are different traditional preparations to be used, the dose, plant part used and the duration of use. It is therefore essential to carefully document traditional knowledge and experiences of A. esculentus, to standardise the plant chemically, to carry out mechanistic studies, toxicological evaluation and clinical tests under controlled conditions to ensure that traditional usage of the plant can be scientifically validated and used as a therapeutic agent [14].

IV. NUTRITIONAL AND BIOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION

Abelmoschus esculentus is known to be a very popular vegetable and a rich source of nutritional components, exhibiting a notable biochemical diversity. Edible pods, seeds, leaves and other parts of the plants have a wide range of macronutrients, micronutrients, dietary fibre, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals. The composition of okra can vary according to cultivar, geographical origin, maturity stage, farming operations, environmental conditions and postproduction treatments. These nutritional and biochemical properties have significant impact on the nutritional value of this product as a functional food, and could serve as the basis for many other reported pharmacological properties. Immature pods have a relatively high moisture content and low energy density and are useful for use in balanced diets. One of the significant nutritional factors are carbohydrates, but a large portion of the carbohydrate fraction comes from complex polysaccharides and dietary fibre sources. Also, okra is a good source of protein, and it contains almost no fat. Its low calorie density and significant fibre content make it a key component in dietary plans focused on weight management, blood sugar control, and heart health [15]. A. esculentus is one of the most significant nutritional characteristics of dietary fibre. The fibre is comprised of soluble fibre and insoluble fibre. The soluble portion is closely linked with the characteristic mucilage of the pods, and the insoluble fibre has the effect of increasing the bulk of the gut and regularity of the

Okra mucilage consists primarily of complex polysaccharides made up of different sugars like galactose, rhamnose and galacturonic acid in different amounts. This mucilage is thick, and can affect gastrointestinal transit and nutrient absorption. It has thus spurred interest in its possible use as a postprandial glucose-lowering agent, as a lipid absorption inhibitor and as a gastrointestinal health aid. Immature pods are of moderate protein content while the seeds have significantly higher protein content and are considered a potential source of plant based protein. There are several essential and non-essential amino acids in okra seed proteins. The seeds have a nutritional value due to their amino acid composition and have been of interest due to their potential as an alternative protein source. Oil also makes up a significant proportion of the seeds. Okra seed oil mainly consists of unsaturated and saturated fatty acids, such as linoleic acid, oleic acid, and palmitic acid. The seed fraction has additional nutritional value due to the presence of polyunsaturated fatty acids [16]. A. esculentus is also an important source of vitamins. Fresh pods are rich in vitamin C, which is important for antioxidant defence, immune and connective tissue function. Another nutritionally important component is folate, which is especially important to DNA synthesis, cellular division and maternal nutrition. The pods also have provitamin A carotenoids and minor levels of some B-complex vitamins. Their levels can decrease during extended storage or during high-temperature processing, highlighting the need for proper handling and preparation. The mineral content of okra also adds to its nutritional value. Minerals reported throughout the plant include calcium, potassium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron, zinc and manganese. Potassium and magnesium are especially significant for cardiovascular and neuromuscular health; calcium and phosphorus for skeletal health. Iron is involved in oxygen transport and many enzymatic reactions, while zinc and manganese are also factors in many enzymes that are involved in metabolic function and as antioxidant enzymes. The nutritional levels (e.g. mineral concentrations) of pods, leaves and seeds can vary significantly, where the seed may have a comparatively high profile of nutrients [17]. A. esculentus is loaded with biologically active phytochemicals other than nutrients. The most common of the constituents investigated are polyphenolics, flavonoids and phenolic acids. Quercetin and its glycosides are known to be associated with okra along with other glycosidic derivatives of flavonoids. The compounds could be responsible for the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity that has been reported for okra extracts. Phenolics are able to act as antioxidants, chelators, and regulators of intracellular signalling pathways involved in oxidative stress and inflammatory responses. The plant is also rich in biochemical compounds, comprising carotenoids, chlorophylls, sterols, tannins and other minor phytoconstituents. These compounds are of variable relative abundance depending upon the plant part and developmental stage. For instance, the leaves may have more phenolics and pigments in them, while the seeds contain more proteins, lipids and sterol-related compounds. These differences are significant in determining the medicinal characteristics of particular extracts or fractions. The other important characteristic of okra is its content of antinutritional factors which vary in quantity. Certain minerals can become less bioavailable when present with compounds like phytates, oxalates and tannins at high concentrations. Some of these components can be reduced during common processing methods such as soaking, cooking, fermentation, and thermal processing. Thus, in general, the nutritional properties of okra are significantly better than its antinutrient properties if used as a regular food [18]. It can be concluded that the nutritional and biochemical profile of A. esculentus is very similar to its nutritional and medicinal importance. The fibre-rich mucilage, vitamins, minerals, seed proteins, fatty acids and phytochemicals in its composition offer a biochemical foundation for its potential metabolic regulatory, antioxidant, digestive and chronic disease prevention properties. Additional specific nutritional and biochemical standardization and comparison of cultivars and plant parts could enhance the knowledge on the contribution of specific nutritional and biochemical constituents to the pharmacological potential of this versatile species.

Qualitative and quantitative distribution of these constituents varies with cultivar, plant part, maturity, environment, geographical origin, extraction method, and post harvest processing. They can regulate oxidative-stress related enzymes and inflammatory signalling pathways, which is significant in their involvement in the potential therapeutic efficacy of okra in chronic metabolic disorders [21]. 5.3 Polysaccharides and Mucilage The mucilaginous texture of okra is a result of the presence of complex water-soluble polysaccharides. These macromolecules are one of the most unique phytochemicals of the plant. The Okra mucilage is made up of various monosaccharide units arranged in the form of complex polymeric structure such as rhamnose, galactose and galacturonic acid. These polysaccharides have been of interest for their physicochemical properties, especially their water holding capacity and viscosity, for pharmaceutical and nutritional applications. From a biological perspective, okra polysaccharides have been explored for the their potential antihyperglycemic, immunomodulatory, antioxidant, gastroprotective, and prebiotic properties. They can thicken the contents of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which may help to delay the absorption of glucose and thereby improve postprandial glucose control. Furthermore, mucilage can serve to make natural thickener, stabiliser and/or delivery agent for drugs [22]. 5.4 Tannins Tannins are polyphenolic compounds, which have been identified in different parts of A. esculentus, especially in seeds and leaves. These compounds have a protein binding and astringent property and may have antioxidant and antimicrobial activity. It is also possible that tannins affect digestive enzymes and nutrient absorption. While moderate levels of dietary intake can be beneficial, high concentrations can result in less bioavailability of proteins and minerals. The activity of okra thus depends on its concentration, plant part and its method of preparation. 5.5 Terpenoids and Sterols Terpenoid and phytosterol constituents are also found in okra. Structurally, plant sterols resemble cholesterol, and can be involved in the plant's ability to lower lipids by blocking cholesterol absorption in the gut. The seed fractions rich in sterols, therefore, have been the subject of study with regard to dyslipidemia and cardiovascular protection. Terpenoid compounds are less well-studied than flavonoids and polysaccharides, but can be involved in antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects. 5.6 Carotenoids and Pigments The green pods and leaves of A. esculentus contain the majority of carotenoids. These pigments also contain provitamin A and non-provitamin A carotenoids which have antioxidant effects and are important for nutrition. The chlorophylls are also present in large amounts in green tissues and give the green colour to fresh pods and leaves. Concentrations of pigment vary from cultivar to cultivar, as well as depending on storage, maturity and cooking. Carotenoids could provide antioxidant effects that are synergistic with the antioxidant activity of the phenolic compounds/f flavonoids [23-25]. 5.7 Other Minor Phytoconstituents Besides the major groups mentioned above, okra contains other low molecular weight components such as organic acids, saponins, amino-acid derivatives, volatile compounds, etc. Bioactive peptides and seed-associated compounds with potential antioxidant and/or metabolic activity have also been identified in some studies. Though they may occur in small amounts, they may interact additively or synergistically to add to the biological activity associated with them. The phytochemical profile varies greatly between the different parts of A. esculentus. The pods have a higher mucilage, soluble polysaccharide, phenolics, and flavonoids content while seeds have more proteins, oils, sterols, and some phenolics. Leaves usually contain high amounts of flavonoids, pigments, and antioxidants, and the flowers can have more phenolic and flavonoid derivatives. The metabolites of roots are comparatively less studied and also have biologically relevant metabolites [26]. In general, the phytochemical profile of A. esculentus is highly complex and diverse. The pharmacological activity does not seem to be reliant on a single active compound but rather, on the synergistic effect of multiple classes of phytoconstituents. So, a thorough phytochemical profiling, quantitative standardization and marker compound characterization are therefore indispensable for establishing reliable correlations between chemical composition and therapeutic activity.

VI. PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTIVITIES

The diverse phytochemical constituents of Abelmoschus esculentus have caught a lot of pharmacological attention due to the flavonoids, phenolic acids, polysaccharides, mucilage, sterols, tannins, carotenoids, and other bioactive constituents present in it. Experimental investigation with various parts of okra, extracts, fractions and isolated compounds revealed that okra displays wide spectrum of biological activity. The effects are mostly associated with modulation of oxidative stress, inflammatory signalling, glucose and lipid metabolism, cellular defence mechanisms, tissue protection mentioned in Table 2 [27]. 6.1 Antioxidant activity The antioxidant activity is one of the consistently reported pharmacologic properties of A. esculentus. Pod extracts and extracts from the pods and seeds have shown free radical scavenging and reducing properties in various experimental systems, while extracts from the pods and leaves have yielded the same activity in the leaf. The flavonoids, phenolic acids, carotenoids and other polyphenolic compounds are responsible for these effects. Quercetin derivatives and related phytochemicals can scavenge the ROS and inhibit the lipid peroxidation. The antioxidant defence system of the body was also reported to be improved in the case of okra extracts which have been observed to increase the activity of antioxidant enzymes like superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione-related system. These mechanisms suggest that A. esculentus could offer a therapeutic benefit to prevent oxidative damage to cells and tissues in metabolic, inflammatory, hepatic, renal, and neurodegenerative diseases [28]. 6.2 Anti-inflammatory activity The anti-inflammatory effect of okra seems to be related to its antioxidant phytochemicals and polysaccharides. The results of the experimental studies indicate that A. esculentus extracts could inhibit the production of pro-inflammatory mediators and cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. These effects may be mediated by NF-κB pathway inhibition. The anti-oxidative and antiinflammatory effects of okra can help protect against chronic low-grade inflammation, which is associated with diabetes, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and tissue damage [29]. 6.3 Antidiabetic and antihyperglycemic activity One of the most widely studied medicinal properties of A. esculentus is its antidiabetic effects. The glucose lowering activity has been demonstrated in experimental models of diabetes with pod, peel, seed extract and whole fruit extracts. There are a number of processes that could account for this activity. Soluble fibre, mucilage, and polyphenols can help to increase the viscosity of the intestines and slow down the absorption of glucose, whereas polyphenols may inhibit enzymes that break down carbohydrates, like alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase. The phytochemicals present in okra can also help in enhancing insulin sensitivity, utilize glucose more efficiently in peripheral tissues and help lower oxidative damage in the peripheral and pancreatic tissues. All these may indicate the potential of okra to be used as a functional food ingredient for glycemic management, but further clinical investigations are required [30]. 6.4 Antihyperlipidemic activity In a few experimental studies, okra has been shown to have lipid-lowering effect. Okra extracts or dietary supplements have been linked with lower total cholesterol, triglycerides, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, and perhaps higher high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels. Soluble fibre may bind bile acids and cholesterol in the gut, which could decrease their absorption and increase their elimination. Polyphenols can also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and phytosterols can inhibit cholesterol absorption in the gut. These actions may account for the potential role of A. esculentus for dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk reduction [31]. 6.5 Anti obesity activity Due to the fibre content of okra, combined with its metabolic bioactives, it has been the topic of research for its anti-obesity effects. Dietary fibre may be beneficial in making the person full, slowing stomach emptying, and preventing over-consumption of energy. Experimental models have shown that extracts from okra have been linked to an improvement in body weight gain, glucose metabolism, lipid accumulation, and insulin resistance. Other contributing factors may be activation or modulation of metabolic pathways related to fatty-acid oxidation and energy homeostasis. Thus, A. esculentus could affect more than just obesity, and therefore, the mechanism of action for obesity remains a mystery [32]. 6.6 Cardioprotective activity The cardioprotective efficacy of okra may be linked to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, antihyperlipidemic and metabolic effects. Endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular damage are important consequences of oxidative stress and inflammation, and phytochemicals found in okra could help to inhibit these. There is potential for further reduction of cardiovascular risk through improvement of lipid profile and glycemic control. Experimental results have also indicated protection against oxidative myocardial damage, and preservation of endogenous antioxidant enzymes. Taken together these effects may be used to further explore the potential of okra as a therapeutic functional food for the cardiovascular system [33]. 6.7 Antihypertensive activity Initial research shows that A. esculentus might be helpful with lowering blood pressure. This effect could be attributed to endothelial function, antioxidant activity, modulation of vascular tone and the content of potassium and other nutritionally relevant minerals. Some bioactive peptides and phytochemicals could also have a role in the regulation of blood pressure enzymes. The antihypertensive evidence is not as comprehensive as for antidiabetic and antioxidant effects, however, and there is a need for additional mechanistic and clinical investigations [34]. 6.8 Hepatoprotective activity The hepatoprotective activity of okra extract has been demonstrated in the experimental models of chemical and metabolic induced liver damage. It has been linked to decreased liver enzyme abnormalities, lipid peroxidation, oxidative stress and inflammatory changes. The flavonoids and phenols could have a beneficial effect in protecting hepatocyte membranes and enhancing endogenous antioxidant defence, whereas the polysaccharides could provide further anti-inflammatory properties. Okra preparation can decrease oxidative damage, increase the antioxidant enzyme activity, and restrain inflammatory injury in renal tissues. Better blood glucose and lipid metabolism may also help to minimize secondary renal stresses in metabolic disorders. Others report biochemical parameters of renal function may be normalised after treatment with okra extracts. 6.10 Anti-inflammatory activity The mucilage of A. esculentus is a potent justification for the use of this plant traditionally in the gastrointestinal system. The viscous polysaccharides may coat and protect the mucous membranes and may help to maintain the integrity of the mucous membrane, possibly lessening the irritation. Experimental research indicates that okra preparations can help alleviate gastrointestinal inflammation, exert antioxidant effects and reduce gastric damage. Polyphenols can also play a role by helping to reduce oxidative stress and promote tissue repair. These co-operative effects can serve as a logical basis for gastroprotective and anti-ulcer effects [36]. 6.11 Antimicrobial activity The various extracts of okra exhibited antimicrobial activity against some bacterial species. The products of secondary metabolism (phenolic compounds, flavonoids, tannins) can interact with the bacterial cell membranes, enzymes or metabolic processes. Antimicrobial activity has been found to be variable as per plant part, solvents, concentration and microbial strains tested. The results suggest a potential, but okra cannot be recommended as a stand-alone treatment at this time as an alternative to proven antimicrobial treatment [37]. 6.12 Antifungal activity Extracts of several A. esculentus species have also been reported to have antifungal properties. Bioactive compounds could act against the fungi by affecting the integrity of the membrane or the metabolic processes. The extracts from the seed and leaves have been attracting special interest in preliminary screening studies. Evidence is, however, relatively scarce and detailed characterization of antifungal constituents and their mechanism is needed for therapeutic significance [38]. 6.13 Anticancer and cytotoxic activity Okra has anticancer potential, selected cancer cell models demonstrated cytotoxic or growth inhibitory effects of extracts and isolated phytoconstituents. The proposed mechanisms are induction of apoptosis, inhibition of cell proliferation, regulation of oxidative stress, and inhibition of the survival signalling pathways of cancer cells. Some lectin-like proteins and polyphenolic compounds are also potentially interesting for their anti-proliferative properties. But the data in most instances are restricted to in vitro or early preclinical investigations, and definite conclusions about clinical anticancer activity are not yet possible [39]. 6.14 Neuroprotective activity The antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties are likely to be the mechanism of action behind the neuroprotective effects of okra. Several neurological disorders are characterized by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation. The phytochemicals present in okra can help maintain the integrity of neural cells by lowering the levels of reactive oxygen species and also by encouraging the normal antioxidant mechanisms. With better metabolic control, indirectly benefits to the neurological system may also occur, especially in diabetes associated cognitive dysfunction. However, the study of A. esculentus for its neuroprotective effects is still in an early stage of development [40]. 6.15 Immunomodulatory activity Immune-modulatory properties of polysaccharides and polyphenolic constituents of okra have been studied. These compounds could alter the activities of macrophages, cytokine production and cellular immune responses. Okra polysaccharide can augment protective immune activity in some experiments, and diminish excess inflammatory signalling in others. Dual regulatory effects are of interest in conditions where there is immune imbalance, but the characterization of the specific active molecules should be continued [41]. 6.16 Wound-healing activity The wound healing property of A. esculentus might be attributed to its antioxidant, anti-microbial, antiinflammatory and mucilage properties. Leaves, pods or mucilage can be used to make topical treatments that can help keep the skin moist, prevent skin damage and promote skin repair. The antioxidant activity can decrease the oxidative damage at the wound site while antimicrobial activity can help to prevent microbial proliferation. Experimental observations indicate that there are wound contraction and tissue regeneration improvements, but that standardised formulations and clinical evaluation are required [42]. 6.17 Reproductive and fertility-related effects The effects of okra on reproductive function are not so well understood and may vary by part of the plant, dose, duration and experimental model. Its actions on reproductive hormones, sperm characteristics, oxidative stress and reproductive-organ function have been investigated in some studies. The antioxidant components could help to prevent oxidative damage to the reproductive tissues, while the nutritional components could aid in normal physiological function. On the other hand, reports on concentrated extracts emphasize the importance of careful assessment of reproductive safety. Thus, reproductive and fertility effects should be approached with some caution until further uniform mechanistic and toxicological data are available [43].

VII. MOLECULAR MECHANISMS AND SIGNALLING PATHWAYS

The pharmacologic effects of Abelmoschus esculentus are currently linked to regulation of several molecular targets instead of one single target. The phytochemicals, such as flavonoids, phenolic acids, polysaccharides, mucilage-derived carbohydrates, sterols and others can affect oxidative stress, inflammation, glucose and lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and intestinal microbial balance. This multitarget behaviour is especially significant in chronic diseases, like diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular diseases, inflammatory diseases and cancer, where multiple intertwined signalling networks play a role in the evolution of the disease [45]. 7.1 Regulation of Oxidative Stress and the Nrf2/HO-1 Pathway Oxidative stress is the imbalanced production of ROS and the endogenous antioxidant defence. Phytoconstituents from A. esculentus such as polyphenols and flavonoids might help prevent oxidative damage by directly scavenging free radicals and/or by regulating antioxidant mechanisms within the cells. One of the key mechanisms is the transcription factor nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) which regulates the expression of antioxidant and cytoprotective genes. In the presence of oxygen, activation and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 activate genes that encode enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione-related enzymes and NADPH quinone oxidoreductase-1. The phytochemicals present in okra may help enhance this line of defence, which can alleviate lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation, and cellular damage. The hepatoprotective, nephroprotective, cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects of A. esculentus have been reported, which in part could be attributed to the enhancement of the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway [46]. 7.2 Modulation of NF-κB-mediated inflammation Nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) is a key player in inflammatory responses and acts as a regulator of the transcription of many genes that regulate cytokine production, immune-cell activation and tissue injury. Increased and sustained NF-κB activation has been linked to chronic inflammatory diseases, insulin resistance, obesity, cardiovascular disease, and carcinogenesis. The polyphenolic and flavonoid profile of okra can help to inhibit overactive activation of NF-κB by inhibiting upstream oxidative signals and disrupting inflammatory signalling pathways. The decreased activity of NF-κB may then lead to a decrease in the expression of inflammatory mediators including cyclooxygenase-2, inducible nitric oxide synthase and a number of proinflammatory cytokines. This mechanism establishes an important connection between antioxidant and antiinflammatory properties of A. esculentus, since the antioxidant activity can indirectly help to decrease inflammation [47]. 7.3 Effects on inflammatory cytokines Chronic inflammation and metabolic dysfunction are regulated by inflammatory cytokines, namely tumour necrosis factor (TNF)–α, interleukin (IL)– 1β and IL-6. These mediators can prevent insulin action, injure the endothelial cells, cause inflammation in the liver and lead to tissue damage when present in excess amounts. Experimental studies indicate that okra extracts might suppress the production/activation of these cytokines. The effects can be due to the inhibition of NFκB and other inflammatory pathways along with a decrease in oxidative stress. Macrophage activation and immune signalling may also be affected by the polysaccharide. A. esculentus has the capability of decreasing the activity of pro-inflammatory cytokines, thereby creating a more balanced inflammatory environment in metabolic and inflammatory diseases [48]. 7.4 Regulation of glucose metabolism and insulin signalling The anti-diabetic effect of A. esculentus seems to be involved in both gastrointestinal and intracellular pathway. Soluble fibre and mucilage in the pods may lead to slower gastric emptying and slow down the absorption of glucose in the intestine. Besides, some phytochemicals could inhibit the activity of carbohydrate-digesting enzymes like α-amylase and α-glucosidase, which could help lower the postprandial glucose level. The okraderived compounds might enhance insulin sensitivity and facilitate the uptake of glucose in peripheral tissues at the cellular level. This could include the regulation of insulin receptor signalling and the downstream pathways like phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt), which is crucial for the translocation of the glucose transporters and glucose utilization. The reduction of oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokines could further enhance insulin signalling, as both are important factors in insulin resistance [49].

AMPK promotes glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial energy production, and inhibits fatty-acid synthesis and hypergluconeogenesis. Concentrations of bioactive compounds in A. esculentus could potentially modulate the AMPK-related pathways, especially in cases of obesity, insulin resistance, and metabolic stress. AMPK activation has the ability to reduce hepatic glucose production, increase insulin sensitivity and inhibit enzymes responsible for the synthesis of fatty-acids and cholesterol. It is hypothesised that these mechanisms may be responsible for the reported anti-obesity, antihyperglycaemic and anti-hyperlipidemic activity of okra. However, the direct evidence of the individual okra phytoconstituents acting as AMPK activators is still not well understood and needs to be studied in detail [50]. 7.6 Modulation of lipid metabolism The anti-lipid activity of A. esculentus occurs in both the gut and liver. Soluble dietary fibre will chelate bile acids and inhibit cholesterol absorption in the intestine, which will help to promote cholesterol excretion. Phytosterols also can be inhibitory to the absorption of dietary cholesterol. Okra phytochemicals could act at a metabolic level to affect pathways of lipid synthesis, fatty-acid oxidation, and lipoprotein metabolism. AMPK mediated regulation can potentially inhibit lipogenic enzymes, while enhanced insulin sensitivity may help to decrease abnormal liver lipid accumulation. Antioxidants can also help prevent lowdensity lipoprotein (LDL) from oxidizing, a factor in atherosclerosis. These synergistic effects suggest that okra can have a beneficial effect on the circulating lipid profile and decrease the metabolic stress of dyslipidemia [51]. 7.7 Apoptosis and cell-cycle regulation in cancer Early research indicates that some of the compounds found in A. esculentus can interfere with the growth of cancer cells, helping to induce cell death and disrupt the cell cycle. De controled apoptosis is regulated by the balance between pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins, the integrity of the mitochondria, activation of caspases and some intracellular signalling pathways. The flavonoids, phenolics and proteinaceous constituents in okra have been studied for their potential against inhibiting the viability of cancer cells. The mechanisms suggested are enhancement of pro-apoptotic signalling, activation of caspases, disruption of the mitochondrial membrane and modulation of Bcl-2 family proteins. Other extracts can also affect the cell-cycle checkpoints and decrease the progression through the proliferative stages. Blocking inflammatory and oxidative signalling may yield further anti-cancer benefits, particularly in cases of NF-κB and associated pathways survival of tumour cells. They are rather preliminary results and should be viewed as a proxy for clinical anticancer efficacy [52]. 7.8 Mitochondrial protective mechanisms The mitochondria play a key role in energy production, oxidative metabolism, apoptosis and cellular stress responses. An excess of ROS may cause damage to the cell's DNA, protein and mitochondrial membranes, resulting in decreased ATP production and cell death. Mitochondrial dysfunction is responsible for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hepatic injury, renal dysfunction and neurodegeneration. The antioxidant properties of A. esculentus could help prevent oxidative damage and maintain the integrity of mitochondrial membrane functions. The boosting of endogenous antioxidant defense can help lower the generation of ROS in mitochondria, and the improvement of metabolic regulation can help lower excess substrate overload. Mitochondrial function preservation can be therefore responsible for the tissue protective effect of okra noted in experimental models. The interconnected nature of these mechanisms is seen from the fact that activation of Nrf2, AMPK signalling and inhibition of inflammatory pathways are all interconnected with mitochondrial regulation [53]. 7.9 Gut microbiota related mechanisms The gut microbiota plays an important role in regulating metabolic, immune and inflammatory health, and is now a well-recognized factor. The indigestible polysaccharides and dietary fibre in A. esculentus can reach the colon where they can be used as substrates for microbial fermentation. This makes it likely that okra has some biological effects that occur in a prebiotic-like manner. The fermentation of fibre can lead to the generation of short-chain fatty acids like acetate, propionate and butyrate that affect intestinal barrier function, glucose metabolism, modulation of immune system and energy balance [54]. It is also possible that okra polysaccharides could change the relative abundance of good and bad bacteria. New bacterial balance can help decrease intestinal inflammation, endotoxin-induced metabolic stress and maintain mucosal integrity. These gut mediated effects of okra may account, in part, for its antidiabetic, anti-obesity, and anti-inflammatory effects. In general, the molecular pharmacology of A. esculentus seems to be a complex interplay between various antioxidant, inflammatory, metabolic, mitochondrial, and apoptotic pathways and gut microbiota-related pathways. Many of the biological effects have been reported and might be explained by activation of Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defence, inhibition of NF-κB signalling, regulation of inflammatory cytokines, improvement of insulin and AMPK pathways, modulation of lipid metabolism and protection of mitochondrial function [55].

VIII. FUTURE PERSPECTIVES

The scientific interest of the Abelmoschus esculentus increases, due to its functional food, nutraceutical and pharmacologically active properties. Future work should go beyond extract based work to identification, isolation and standardization of specific bioactive constituents that brings about the biological effects of the plant. Flavonoids, phenolic compounds, polysaccharides, mucilage, phytosterols and bioactives derived from the seeds are of particular consideration. The relations between phytoconstituents and molecular targets could be more precisely established by applying advanced analytical approaches such as metabolomics, LC-MS/MS, molecular docking, network pharmacology and systems biology.
