Vol:.(1234567890) Plant Molecular Biology Reporter (2025) 43:602–616 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11105-024-01484-z RESEARCH Approach of Genetic Diversity of Lippia alba (Mill) and Petiveria alliacea L.: Medicinal Plants of Colombia Lina Tarazona‑Pulido1,2 · Paula Andrea Rugeles‑Silva1,2 · Karen Melissa Cardona Tobar1,2 · Lucía Ana Díaz‑Ariza2 · Jaime Eduardo Muñoz Florez1 · Diana López‑Álvarez1 Received: 5 February 2024 / Accepted: 15 July 2024 / Published online: 29 August 2024 © The Author(s) 2024 Abstract The medicinal Lippia alba and Petiveria alliacea, originating from Central and South America, exhibit a wide range of beneficial properties, including antimicrobial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, antitumor, analgesic, and antibacterial effects. However, little is known about their population structure and genetic diversity, which may hinder the establishment of their cultivation in different regions of Colombia. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the genetic diversity and population structure of 17 samples of L. alba from the departments of Tolima, Valle del Cauca, and Putumayo, as well as 31 samples of P. alliacea from the departments of Cundinamarca, Boyacá, Tolima, and Valle del Cauca. We employed restriction-site associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) with the enzyme PstI. We performed denovo_map and ref_map pipeline for L. alba and identified a total of 17,036 loci and 14,562 SNPs, respectively, revealing a genetic variation of 5.19% (FST of 0.05; p < 0.001) among its populations and two delimited genetic groups. For P. alliacea, in denovo_map our analysis discovered 6395 SNPs, indicating substantial genetic variation of 75% among the studied populations (FST = 0.75; p < 0.001), resulting in the delineation of four genetic groups. Our findings will contribute to providing valuable molecular data on the populations of these medicinal plants and provide evidence of the genetic flow existing among L. alba populations, while P. alliacea populations are more structured. We also performed a FDIST analysis; for L. alba using the results with reference, we identified 37 SNPs coding for proteins in biological, molecular, and cellular processes; and finally, we highlighted the gene SASPL_104284 involved in metabolic processes. Keywords RADseq · PstI · Omics · SNPs · Genetic diversity · Population structure Introduction The knowledge of medicinal plants in Colombia can be traced back to traditional practices of ethnic groups and tribes, that have passed down this information from generation to generation. This knowledge is supported by ethnopharmacological studies (Gómez-Estrada et al. 2011) and chemical studies that evaluate the presence of secondary metabolites with pharmacological potential in their extracts (Muñoz-Acevedo et al. 2019). On the other hand, studies on their genetics are scarce, and in some cases, nonexistent. Considering that the study of genetic diversity within and among individuals and species in a population allows us to understand the processes of selection and evolution of populations (Salgotra and Chauhan 2023), as well as serving as a starting point for future studies that seek to understand the mechanism by which genes involved in the synthesis of secondary metabolites function, it is essential to conduct Key Message • In this research, we present an approach to genomic analysis of different populations of L. alba and P. alliacea in Colombia; we found that the first exhibits lower population structure and greater genetic diversity within populations, and the second shows greater structure among populations. * Diana López‑Álvarez

The results here obtained could advance our knowledge of these plants and help in selecting superior genotypes that could be used in the establishment of crops aimed at conserving, studying, or utilizing their potential. To conduct these genetic analyses, different molecular and biotechnological technologies and methodologies have been developed, allowing for an in-depth exploration of the genetic structure and sequence of a species of interest (Scheben et al. 2017). One sequencing (NGS) is Restriction Site Associated DNA Sequencing (RADseq), which can offer valuable information insight into species genomes at a reduced cost compared to complete sequencing. RADseq uses a specific restriction endonuclease to digest DNA into short fragments, enabling de novo analysis that takes advantage of the data’s reduced complexity to discover reference-free variants and genotype them (Peterson et al. 2014). This technique allows for the identification of Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs), which are considered abundant and high-density genetic markers, making it an ideal tool for evaluating and understanding the genetic and structural mechanisms of genomic regions in different species and their populations (Baird et al. 2008). Currently, the interest in studying medicinal plants has increased due to their use as therapeutic strategies for various diseases such as cancer. In Colombia, the GAT program (Generation of therapeutic alternatives in cancer from plants) aims to study the genetic diversity of different species that could have antitumor or anticancer activity, such as Lippia alba (Mill) and Petiveria alliacea, natives of Tropical and Subtropical America, that in Colombia they can be found in domesticated wild or environments throughout all geographic regions. Lippia alba (Mill.) N.E.Br. ex Britton and P. Wilson (Lamiales: Verbenaceae), known by common names in Spanish of “Pronto alivio,” “Alivia dolor,” and “Curalo todo” (Bernal et al. 2017), is a subshrub or shrub and grows primarily in the seasonally dry tropical biome, ranging from 400 to 2120 masl, has a maximum height of up to 2 m, and has pedunculated lilac or white inflorescences. It is categorized as “Least Concern” (LC) by The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and on Colombia’s National Red List (Muñoz et al. 2007; ColPlantA 2023). Natural populations of this species are allogamous, self-incompatible, and traditionally reproduced by cuttings (Venâncio et al. 2016). A total of eighteen metabolites have been identified, with key compounds including monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, essential oils, carvone, limonene, flavonoids, alkaloids, phenols, tannins, and saponins (Ministerio de Protección Social 2008); these compounds can be present in the essential oils of the plant and which vary significantly according to the plant’s ploidy level (Lopes et al. 2020) which has been described as an autopolyploid complex with five cytotypes (2n = 30, 38, 45, 60, and 90) (de Souza et al. 2021). Using flow cytometry, it has been described as having a genetic size of 2,234 Mb (Leitch et al. 2019) and genome annotation (ASM3783412v1) at the scaffold level with a size of 689.1 Mb and 449,796 scaffold count was recently published. Traditionally, L. alba has been used for various medicinal purposes (Cardona et al. 2024), including treating digestive system ailments such as diarrhea and colic, functioning as an analgesic or antiseptic for colds, acting as an expectorant for allergies, and addressing menstrual disorders, hypertension, anemia, and skin diseases (Pedro et al. 2014; Buitrago Zapata et al. 2018; Pájaro-González et al. 2022). It is attributed with various pharmacological potentials, including antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, antiprotozoal, neurosedative, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-spasmodic, and cytotoxic activities depending on the method of administration, either by infusion or maceration. In Colombia, it is recognized by “Instituto Nacional de Vigilancia de Medicamentos y Alimentos” (INVIMA) in the list of medicinal plants for therapeutic purposes as an external antiseptic (Buitrago Zapata et al. 2018; INVIMA 2018; Coronel Alva and Zevallos Escobar 2019). On the other hand, the specie Petiveria alliacea L. (Caryophyllales: Petiveraceae), known by common names in Spanish of “Anamú,” “Chimú,” “Mucura,” “Mucuracá,” “Palindera,” “Namú,” “Lancetilla,” “Mapurite,” or “fimercarra” (Bernal et al. 2017). It is a subshrub or shrub and grows primarily in the wet tropical biome and can be found in Colombia both in the wild and cultivated, ranging from 5 to 1780 masl. This plant maintains a “Least Concern” (LC) conservation status according to the IUCN and features on Colombia’s National Red List (ColPlantA 2023). It has a maximum height of up to 1.5 m and can reproduce sexually or asexually, typically being self-pollination. Its flowers are white and arranged in terminal clusters. A total of 14 secondary metabolites have been identified, primarily encompassing alkaloids, flavonoids, triterpenes, tannins, benzoic acid, lignoceric acid, and stearic acid, among others. While the genome size remains unknown and lacks a published reference genome, its chloroplast sequence length measures 154,947 bp (Ministerio de Protección Social 2008; Alarcón Restrepo 2011; PCIDB 2023). Traditionally, it has been used to treat fever, as an antiseptic, anti-inflammatory, and analgesic for skin conditions, and anti-asthma, as an animal abortifacient. Its applications extend to treating sinusitis, arthritis, migraines, anxiety, and epilepsy, with believed effects on memory. Moreover, it is considered to inhibit the metastasis of cancer cells and is included in the list of accepted medicinal plants for therapeutic purposes as an oral mucosal anti-inflammatory (Ministerio de Protección Social 2008; INVIMA 2018; Pájaro-González et al. 2022). Regarding its pharmacological potential, P. alliacea is an agent that prevents tumor proliferation in prostate cancer and myeloblastic leukemia (Ruffa et al. 2002). Its extract has been studied for

Considering the scarcity of genetic information available for these two species, this study aimed to investigate the genetic diversity and population structure of the medicinal plants L. alba and P. alliacea sampled from different departments across Colombia, where the GAT program was interested in establishing crops and where the medicinal use of these plants in the wild was recorded. Materials and Methods Sample Collection, DNA Extraction, and RADseq Library Preparation For the genomic analysis of these species, 20 individuals were collected for L. alba, five (5) were obtained from the Tolima department to 375 masl, municipality of Lérida; six (6) from the Putumayo department to 2,067 masl, municipality of Sibundoy; and nine (9) from the Valle del Cauca department to 978 masl, municipality of Palmira. These latter samples pertain to various locations in Colombia as they are part of a Germplasm Bank for medicinal plants located in the municipality of Palmira (Fig. 1). Regarding P. alliacea, 31 individuals were collected, 16 from the Tolima department to 230 masl, ten (10) from the municipality of Ambalema, and six (6) from the municipality of Armero Guayabal. Additionally, five (5) individuals were collected from the Cundinamarca department to 1329 masl, municipality of Pacho; five (5) from the Boyacá department to 2062 masl, municipality of Villa de Leyva; and five (5) from the Valle del Cauca department to 978 masl, municipality of Palmira (Fig. 1). Of each individual was collected between 3 and 5 leaf samples were, ensuring that these were young leaves or new plant shoots and in good condition, free from signs of predation, fungi, or pathogens. These samples were preserved in paper envelopes accompanied by silica gel to prevent decomposition or fungi growth. Additionally, of each population were deposited one sample collected in the herbarium of Pontificia Universidad Javeriana in Bogotá D.C Fig. 1 Sampling points individuals L. alba and P. alliacea. The genomic DNA (gDNA) was isolated from 100 mg of fresh leaf tissue using Wizard® Genomic DNA Purification (PROMEGA, MD) following the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA concentrations were measured by Qubit 4™ DNA Assays, Kit Qubit™ 1X dsDNA High Sensitivity (HS) Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). The quality of gDNA samples was evaluated using Berthold Technologies Colibri microvolume spectrometer and by 2% agarose gel stained with GelRed DNA stain using the ENDURO™ Gel XL Electrophoresis System; RADseq libraries were constructed using a protocol adapted from Baird et al. (2008), through Floragenex Inc. (Beaverton, Oregon, USA) using the restriction enzyme PstI. The samples were sequenced on an Illumina® NovaSeq 6000 platform to produce 100-bp single-end reads. Bioinformatic Analyses Demultiplexing the Data and SNP Calling The quality of raw reads was assessed using FastQC v 0.12.1 (Wingett and Andrews 2018). The STACKS v 2.64 software pipeline (Catchen et al. 2011) was employed for SNP calling. For the two species, denovo_map pipeline was run; additionally, for L. alba, ref_map was running with its reference genome. Raw reads were demultiplexed using the process_radtags script, and all samples were checked for barcode and RAD cut site integrity. Low-quality reads, defined as those with a Phred score of less than 20, were filtered out. For denovo_map, the ustacks tool uses two main parameters within the process, which affect how loci are constructed within each sample and should be tested considering different decision frameworks (see Supplementary Note 1). Then, the cstacks script generated the catalog of consensus loci by merging the alleles from each population, and comparisons were made between samples from the created catalog using the sstacks tool. Next, gstacks identified and genotyped the SNPs within the metapopulation under the variant calling model and genotype likelihoods (Maruki and Lynch 2017) with a threshold alpha ranging between 0.01 and 0.05 for each locus. The “populations” script then generated VCF (Variant Calling File) output file used for genetic and structure analysis. For pipeline running through ref_map, we aligned our samples with the reference genome of L. alba (ASM3783412v1) using the BWA software (Li and Durbin 2010) before running gstacks and populations tools of Stacks. Additionally, using TASSEL v5 (Bradbury et al. 2007) filtered the VCF file of denovo_map where a locus was required to be present between at least 70 and 80% of the individuals and ref_map for L. alba was required that the locus to be present in 90% of the individuals. Genetic Diversity Analyses The genetic diversity of the natural populations was assessed by estimating observed heterozygosity (Ho), expected heterozygosity (He), transition and transversions numbers, nucleotide compositions and diversity (Pi), and number of polymorphic sites using Tajima D test (Tajima 1989); we evaluated the molecular indices Theta S (ΘS) and Theta Pi (Θπ) which represents the distribution of variation within or between populations based on polymorphic sites, values of inbreeding coefficient (FIS), and HW test in Arlequin v 3.5.2.2 (Excoffier and Lischer 2010); we also analyzed the gene flow level among all populations with the Nm parameter using equation Nm = (1-Fst)/(4Fst). Population Structure and Phylogeny Three distinct methods were used to ascertain the genetic structure of the populations. First, ADMIXTURE v 1.3.0 (Excoffier and Lischer 2010) was employed, utilizing the maximum likelihood algorithm to explore the genetic structure of the data. Ten independent runs were performed for each K value, from 1 to 5 for L. alba and from 1 to 6 for P. alliacea. To visualize the optimal number of delta K values and the model of population structure, the .Q and .P files were used as input in the software STRU​CTU​RE SELECTOR (Li and Liu 2018), along with a population map. Second, we performed a principal component analysis (PCA) using the SNPrelate v 1.34.1. (Zheng et al. 2012) package and ggplot2 v 3.4.2 (Wickham 2009) in R 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2021) to extract the synthetic variables to represent major genetic variations. Thirdly, a maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic inference was performed using IQ-TREE v 2.1.4 (Minh et al. 2020) with 150,000 bootstrap replicates. The tree was visualized using iTOL v 5 (Letunic and Bork 2021) and the substitution model was determined using the software jModelTest v 2.1.10 (Darriba et al. 2012) employing the Bayesian model selection criterion with support from 24 models provided by default. To evaluate the correlation between the geographical distance and the genetic distance of the populations, a Mantel test was performed using the software IBD (Isolation by Distance) (Bohonak 2002) and an AMOVA test considering Wright’s population structure statistics in Arlequin (Excoffier and Lischer 2010). Finally, an FST outlier approach was used to determine a set of candidate SNPs that had significantly higher FST values than expected under a neutral model of selection using the FDIST (Beaumont and Nichols 1996) implemented in Arlequin. This method detects genes under selection based on the distributions of heterozygosity and FST and can

We selected SNPs that had significantly higher FST values than expected; we ran 10,000 simulations with 100 demes per species and minimum and maximum expected heterozygosities of 0 and 0.8, respectively. We considered markers with FST values higher than 95% (> 0.05) of the neutral distribution were considered to be under divergent selection, and markers with FST lower than 95% of neutral distribution were inferred to be subject to balancing selection (Beaumont and Nichols 1996). Once the SNPs identified under divergent selection were obtained, a BLAST (Altschul et al. 1990) was performed in NCBI and UniProt (The UniProt Consortium 2021) to obtain relevant information about possible genes or proteins that were related to them. Results RADseq Libraries and SNP Calling After sequencing the RAD libraries of the 20 samples from L. alba, we obtained 3.8 GB of raw data consisting of more than 25 million reads measuring 123 bp. The raw data showed high Phred quality Q30 for more than 90% of the samples with an average GC content of 46% (sd. 4.6), and for P. alliacea, we obtained 16 GB of raw data from 31 samples, consisting more of 163 million reads with high Phred quality (Q30 > 90%), 123 bp in length, and an average GC content of 42% (sd. 4.0). For denovo_map assembly, once we established the parameters for ustacks, ran each component individually. For the L. alba, we obtained 78,753,775 RADtags (Supplementary Table 2) that consisted of 2,704,413 RAD loci with an effective per sample mean coverage of 19.3x (min = 14.7x, max = 30.8x), composed of 404,517 variant sites, 196,585 SNPs, and an average of 41,175 private alleles per population (Table 1). After removing SNPs with missing data in TASEEL, 17,036 SNPs were retained in 16 samples. For P. alliacea after assembly, 325,195,434 RADtags were obtained (Supplementary Table 2), forming 1,667,988 RAD loci with an effective per-sample mean coverage of 96.2x (min = 10.5x, max = 445.6x), composed of 172,199 variant sites, 19,491 SNPs, and an average of 17,950 private alleles per population (Table 1). After removing SNPs with missing data in TASSEL, 6395 SNPs were retained in 25 samples. Genetic Differentiation and Analysis of Molecular Variance The population structure was analyzed by an AMOVA. For L. alba, we found that 3.4% of the molecular variation was distributed among populations, while 82.3% from within populations; the fixation indices were FST 0.034 (p < 0.001), FIS 0.147 (p < 0.001), and FIT 0.176 (p < 0.001) (Table 3), with a marked differentiation between populations from Tolima and Putumayo of 0.062 p < 0.001 (Table 4); the Nm parameter was 5 and the Mantel correlation test was r = 0.964 (p = 0.159) indicating a possible correlation between genetic (FST) and geographical distances between populations. On the other hand, the hierarchical AMOVA for P. alliacea showed that 75% of the variance was attributed among populations and 23.6% within individuals; the fixation indices were FST 0.747 (p < 0.001), FIS 0.057 (p < 0.001), and FIT 0.762 (p < 0.001) (Table 3). Genetic differentiation values between population pairs were significant in all comparisons except for those between Cundinamarca and Valle del Cauca (Table 5); the Nm parameter was 0 and the Mantel correlation test was r = 0.439 (p = 0.238) indicating a lack of correlation between genetic and geographical distances between populations. Population Structure The ADMIXTURE population structure analysis of the evaluated species revealed patterns similar to the genetic diversity analyses. For the species L. alba, the three evaluated populations were divided into two optimal genetic groups with a CV of K2: 0.845 (Fig. 3; Supplementary Fig. 2), with some individuals showing a mixture of clusters such as Tol2, Tol-4, VII_1, VII_4, VII_5, and VII_7. However, all individuals from Putumayo, Tol-3, Tol-5, and VII-3 recovered within the same genetic group (Supplementary Table 3). Discussion We consider the results here to be the first record of the genetic diversity and population structure of these two species in Colombia using RADseq methodology. The number of retained reads, loci, and SNPs found in this study are consistent with results reported in other population studies of non-model plants utilizing similar methodologies (Clugston et al. 2019; Palombo and Carrizo García 2022). Furthermore, this study demonstrated that the use of next-generation sequencing methodologies such as RADseq allows for the generation of a high number of single nucleotide polymorphisms, thereby improving genetic analyses. Our study provides evidence supporting the efficiency of Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) in reliably identifying SNPs. The sets of SNPs that we identified proved useful in analyzing the genetic diversity and population structure of the two evaluated medicinal plant species. 613 Plant Molecular Biology Reporter (2025) 43:602–616 across the three evaluated populations, displaying notably higher genetic diversity within these individual populations, for denovo_map and ref_map analysis accounting for approximately 94.8% of the overall variation. Samples from the Tolima and Valle del Cauca populations exhibited potential genetic relatedness, possibly related to the plant’s reproductive modes involving both seeds and cuttings. In contrast, the samples sourced from Putumayo have been propagated via cuttings, potentially impacting the observed population structure evident in our findings. This behavior in the population structure aligns with the molecular indices, notably akin to the populations. Theta Pi values, representing the average number of nucleotide differences per pair, surpassed Theta S values, based on polymorphic sites, for three populations, which corroborates our results by showing greater genetic variation within the population. Additionally, the He values slightly surpassed Ho values, indicating no significant genetic distinctions among these populations. However, a noteworthy and significant genetic distance was discerned between the Tolima and Putumayo populations, accompanied by a higher Ho. Despite this, the nucleotide diversity patterns remained consistent across all populations, with relatively elevated nucleotide transition values. According to Gao et al. (2017), these patterns might be linked to biased mutational processes inherent within plant genomes, for instance, postmeiotic abnormalities affect the formation of viable pollen grains, leading to a significant decrease in L. alba seed germination, thereby posing challenges to its sexual reproduction (Kaur and Singhal 2019). Additionally, there is a unique mode of dissemination where adults from cultural and ethnic groups contribute to dispersal, given its widespread medicinal use and ease of propagation through cuttings or stakes (Herrera-Moreno et al. 2013).On the other hand, for the values Ho higher than He, we can relate them to the opposite phenomenon of the Wahlund effect, which consists of the so-called isolation breakage, where a temporary excess of Ho can occur when geographically isolated populations reproduce (Smith et al. 2020), which can be explained for the L. alba samples. Additionally, the p-value of the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium analysis showed that neither population of the two species is in equilibrium, and the Fis value corroborates the excess of heterozygotes for the Putumayo population for L. alba and the Cundinamarca population for P. alliacea. Previous studies have investigated the genetic diversity of L. alba, utilizing diverse molecular markers. In line with our findings, these studies have reported substantial genetic variation among individuals. Paz Perafán et al. (2019) employed genotyping by GBS and identified 37,917 SNPs, attributing 93.35% of the variation to differences among individuals. Cardona et al. (2019) investigated two ecologically distinct populations (Chicamocha Canyon and the Sumapaz Paramo) using randomly amplified microsatellites (RAMS), observing the highest genetic variation within the assessed populations. Similarly, Julião et al. (2020) analyzed species of Lippia genus using AFLP markers and detected 273 polymorphic loci, delineating three genetic groups among seven studied populations. In this sense, consideration of the high genetic and chemical variability observed in L. alba is essential for establishing conservation plans or germplasm collections that can preserve and represent the variability within this species and be used as a valuable tool for selecting genotypes of interest and reproducing new populations (Manica-Cattani et al. 2009). Furthermore, additional studies focusing on the genetic diversity of L. alba under diverse conditions and within various ecosystems are imperative. Similar congeneric species like L. origanoides have exhibited genetic variation influenced by factors such as altitude, sampling locations, and varying degrees of human impact on their reproductive processes (Vega-Vela and Sánchez 2012). Consequently, exploring these aspects in future studies for L. alba could yield essential insights into its adaptive mechanisms and aid in designing effective conservation and management strategies for this valuable species. The species P. alliacea displayed notable genetic variation, amounting to 75%, observed primarily between populations. Our analysis revealed a robust population structure comprising four distinct genetic groups, indicating limited gene flow between these populations. The Cundinamarca population exhibited a higher count of SNPs and a greater Theta Pi value compared to the other three evaluated populations. However, despite these differences, nucleotide diversity and composition remained consistent across all four populations. In instances where Ho (observed heterozygosity) exceeded He (expected heterozygosity), this discrepancy was observed in the samples from the Cundinamarca and Valle del Cauca populations. Significant genetic distance among the four populations reaffirmed the previously identified population structure. Although studies on the genetics of this species remain limited, other species within the closely related family Phytolaccaceae have recorded polymorphic loci. For instance, using molecular markers such as RAPD, Semagn et al. (2001) estimated a total variance of 17.2% between populations, accompanied by FST values ranging from 0.350 to 0.384. These values signify substantial genetic differentiation between populations, echoing the findings observed in our study among the four evaluated populations. Finally, we can observe that the natural variation, including the genetic variation found in these populations, may lead to various characteristics and genotypic expressions. The SNPs under divergent selection, as classified in the island analysis (FDIST) performed for both species, could be associated with different functional genes involved in the production of secondary metabolites, which confer the pharmacological potential attributed to each of these species.

Plant Molecular Biology Reporter (2025) 43:602–616 We also evidenced that it is necessary to have a reference genome to be able to make an association analysis with the SNPs selected under divergent selection; in the analysis performed for the species L. alba, we also showed that in addition to having an annotation, this should be at the chromosomal level to make a more robust association; however, at a general level, the blast allowed us to identify genes that could be related to biological, molecular, and cellular processes in the species. Conclusions This study revealed genetic differentiation within the studied populations of L. alba, particularly within the populations from Tolima and Valle del Cauca, when compared to the Putumayo population. The reduced diversity and distinct population structure observed in Putumayo might be attributed to this species’ propagation via cuttings in that region. Conversely, P. alliacea displayed a contrasting pattern, showcasing greater genetic variation among populations. This difference in behavior could potentially be linked to the distinct reproductive modes of these species: L. alba predominantly through cuttings in a single population versus P. alliacea potentially through seeds within populations. Moreover, the employed methodology for de novo assembly successfully facilitated the acquisition of genetic diversity and population structure values for the studied populations. These values not only corroborate existing limited information about these species but also introduce a significant number of additional SNPs, substantially expanding the genomic resources available for these species. These expanded resources will enable more comprehensive analyses of genetic diversity and its associations with the production of secondary metabolites responsible for their recognized pharmacological potential. Lastly, this study could serve as a pioneering effort in SNP identification for these two species through the RADseq sequencing methodology. Sci. 31 : 145–155, 2026 doi: 10.11144/Javeriana.SC31.aeop Antineoplastic Effects of Petiveria alliacea: A Systematic Review Protocol Ricardo Ballesteros-Ramírez1,2*, Nicolás Martínez-Ramos1,2, Ginna Paola Fernández Deaza1,2, Eduardo Duque Grisales3, Claudia Lorena Motta Robayo4, Raul Murillo 1,2 Abstract Petiveria alliacea L. (Phytolaccaceae), commonly known as “Anamú” or “Guinea Hen Weed,” is a medicinal plant traditionally used in herbal medicine across Latin America, the Caribbean, and Africa. Preclinical investigations have attributed cytotoxic, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and proapoptotic properties to its bioactive compounds, indicating potential antineoplastic activity. However, available evidence remains fragmented across different experimental models, cancer types, plant preparations, and study designs, and no systematic synthesis of the antineoplastic evidence base has been published to date. This protocol describes the methodology for a systematic review aiming at evaluating the antineoplastic effects of Petiveria alliacea in in vitro cell models, in vivo animal studies, and clinical trials involving cancer patients. Searches will be conducted in ten electronic databases (including MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, LILACS, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SciELO, Epistemonikos, ClinicalTrials.gov, and EudraCT) in English, Spanish, or Portuguese, covering studies published from January 2000 onwards. Eligible studies will include controlled in vitro, in vivo, and clinical investigations reporting antineoplastic outcomes. Study selection will be performed independently by two reviewers using Rayyan. Risk of bias will be assessed using validated tools for preclinical research. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses are planned by tumor type, extract type, plant part, and study model. This protocol was registered in PROSPERO on 26 March 2026 (registration number: CRD420251108791). Keywords: antineoplastic agents; cancer; complementary therapies; petiveria alliacea. 1. Introduction Cancer represents one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with an estimated 20 million new cases and nearly 10 million deaths recorded globally in 2022 [1]. The burden is disproportionately concentrated in low- and middle-income countries, where access to surgery, radiotherapy, and innovative systemic therapies remains severely limited [2]. In this context, plant-derived medicinal products play a prominent role as primary or complementary health resources across diverse cultures, and represent an important reservoir of bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical research [3]. Petiveria alliacea L. (Phytolaccaceae) (known as “Anamú,” “Guinea Hen Weed,” “mucura,” or “tipi”) is a perennial herb indigenous to tropical and subtropical regions of Latin America and the Caribbean, with distribution also documented in Africa. Ethnobotanical records document its widespread traditional use for anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimicrobial, and immunostimulatory purposes [4,5]. Preclinical investigations have associated Petiveria alliacea extracts with inhibition of cancer cell proliferation, induction of apoptosis, antioxidant activity, and reduction of tumor growth in animal models [7,8]. Despite accumulating evidence, investigations have been conducted across heterogeneous cancer types, experimental systems, plant preparations, and outcome measures, preventing the drawing of unified conclusions across studies. To date, no systematic review has comprehensively synthesised the antineoplastic evidence for Petiveria alliacea. This absence limits the ability to identify consistent activity patterns, assess methodological rigor, and guide translational research priorities. This protocol describes the methods for a systematic review aiming at closing this gap, contributing to the evidence base for plant-derived antineoplastic agents and informing future research in integrative oncology. 2. Methods 2.1. Aim and objectives This systematic review aims to evaluate the antineoplastic effects of Petiveria alliacea in in vitro models, in vivo animal studies, and clinical trials. The specific objectives are: • To assess the cytotoxic and antioxidant/prooxidant activity of Petiveria alliacea preparations in in vitro neoplastic cell models, as measured by the inhibitory cytotoxic concentration (IC50) and validated antioxidant assays. • To evaluate the antineoplastic efficacy of Petiveria alliacea in controlled in vivo murine tumor models, based on survival outcomes, treatment response, and tumor suppression. • To summarize available evidence from clinical trials evaluating Petiveria alliacea in cancer patients, including disease-free survival, progression-free survival, overall survival, treatment response rate, and the secondary clinical endpoints: safety and toxicity profiles and health-related quality of life. • To assess the risk of bias and methodological quality of all included studies. • To characterize heterogeneity in Petiveria alliacea preparations and cancer models across included studies, and to identify gaps in the evidence base. 2.2. Study design This review will follow the methodological guidance for systematic reviews of pre-clinical intervention studies, incorporating the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. Risk of bias assessment is based on validated tools for preclinical research. The protocol was registered prospectively in PROSPERO on 26 March 2026 (CRD420251108791) [9]. 2.3. Eligibility criteria 2.3.1. Population and models In vitro studies using established neoplastic cell lines of any type are eligible. In vivo studies in murine models (mice or rats) bearing experimentally induced solid or hematological tumors, with housing conditions and ethical approval, will be included. Clinical studies enrolling adult Universitas Scientiarum:145–155 http://ciencias.javeriana.edu.co/investigacion/universitas-scientiarum

Ballesteros-Ramírez et al., 2026 147 patients (≥18 years) with confirmed cancer diagnosis of any type or stage will also be eligible. Studies using non-murine animal species, healthy animals without neoplastic disease, or pediatric populations will be excluded. 2.3.2. Intervention The intervention of interest is the administration of Petiveria alliacea in any preparation (whole plant, aqueous extract, ethanolic extract, methanolic extract, infusion, or volatile extract), and at any dose. Variable administration routes, frequency, and treatment durations are also acceptable. Studies combining Petiveria alliacea with other agents will be included only when the effects of Petiveria alliacea could be evaluated independently. 2.3.3. Comparator Eligible comparators included vehicle control, untreated cells or animals, placebo, no intervention, or standard antineoplastic therapy. Single-arm studies without a control group will be excluded. 2.3.4. Outcomes Primary outcomes for in vitro studies are IC50 (𝜇g/mL or mg/mL) and antioxidant or prooxidant activity measured by validated assays (ABTS, DPPH, FRAP). Primary outcomes for in vivo and clinical studies are disease-free survival, progression-free survival, overall survival, treatment response rate, and presence of distant metastases. Secondary outcomes included induction of immunogenic cell death markers (ATP depletion, calreticulin expression, HMGB1 release) and changes in metabolic cellular profile. For clinical studies, secondary outcomes also include safety and toxicity profiles (incidence, type, and severity of adverse events) and health-related quality of life, assessed with validated instruments. Studies that do not report any primary antineoplastic outcome will be excluded. 2.3.5. Study design Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled studies, controlled preclinical studies (in vitro and in vivo), semi-experimental animal studies, and controlled clinical cohort studies are eligible. Only original peer-reviewed research articles published from January 2000 onwards in English, Spanish, or Portuguese will be included. Case reports, case series, narrative reviews, scoping reviews, conference abstracts, editorials, letters to the editor, theses, and in silico studies without experimental validation are excluded. 2.4. Search strategy Searches will be conducted in the following electronic databases: MEDLINE (via PubMed), EMBASE (via Embase.com), Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, LILACS (via BVS), ScienceDirect, SciELO, Epistemonikos, ClinicalTrials.gov, and EudraCT. Grey literature will be sought via Google Scholar, Trip Medical Database, Latin American academic repositories, and manual reference checking of included studies. Consistent with the eligibility criteria, only studies published in English, Spanish, or Portuguese will be included; this pragmatic restriction reflects the working languages of the review team and is acknowledged as a minor limitation of the review. Studies published from January 2000 to the date of search will be eligible. Searches were conducted following the PRESS checklist and structured around (i) Petiveria alliacea and its known synonyms combined with controlled vocabulary (MeSH, Emtree, DeCS); and (ii) antineoplastic and cancer-related terms. Strategies were adapted to each database’s syntax and controlled vocabulary. Complete executable search strings, database names, access platforms, search fields, and settings are provided in Supplementary Material (Suppl. 1). 2.5. Study selection The selection of studies will be conducted in three sequential phases: title screening, abstract screening, and full-text review. Each phase will be performed independently by two reviewers using the Rayyan® software [10], with bibliographic fields blinded during title and abstract screening. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus, and a third reviewer will adjudicate unresolved disagreements. Screening decisions and exclusion reasons will be documented according to the PRISMA 2020 flow reporting guideline. Before screening, all records retrieved from the electronic databases will be imported into a reference manager and into Rayyan®, where duplicate records will be removed automatically and then verified manually. When two or more publications report the same experiment or the same patient cohort (companion or redundant reports), the most complete and most recent report will be used as the primary data source and the remaining reports will be linked to it, so that no outcome is counted more than once. 2.6. Data extraction Data extraction will be performed independently by four reviewers using a standardized Microsoft Excel template. At least two reviewers in parallel will extract each study; discrepancies will be resolved by consensus or third-party adjudication. Authors will be contacted by email when essential data are missing or unclear. Variables to be extracted include: bibliographic details; study design and structure; population or model characteristics; intervention details (preparation form, plant part, origin, extraction method, dose, route, frequency, duration); comparator description; and all primary and secondary outcomes with associated statistical measures (mean ± SD, IC50, hazard ratio, confidence interval, p-value). Final data files will be deposited in an open repository upon review completion. 2.7. Risk of bias assessment Bias risk will be assessed independently by three reviewers. For in vivo animal studies, the SYRCLE risk of bias tool [11] and the CAMARADES checklist [12] will be applied. For in vitro studies, the methodological rigor and reporting completeness of each included study will be appraised using the Materials Design, Analysis and Reporting (MDAR) framework and checklist [14], covering key elements such as cell-line authentication, biological and technical replication, statistical reporting, and reagent traceability. For clinical studies, the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool version 2 will be applied to randomized trials, and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to non-randomized studies. A fourth reviewer will arbitrate persistent disagreements. Results will be summarized narratively and presented graphically. Ballesteros-Ramírez et al., 2026 149 2.8. Data synthesis A narrative synthesis will be conducted for all outcomes, providing descriptive summaries and visual representations of the evidence. The pooling of studies will be based on clinical and methodological comparability and assessed via the 𝐼2 statistic. Random-effects models will be used for pooling. Subgroup analyses will be planned by tumor type, extract type, plant part used, and study model. Sensitivity analyses will integrate the exclusion of studies at high risk of bias and of non-randomized studies, where applicable. Potential publication bias will be addressed qualitatively; formal statistical tests will be planned only if 10 or more studies are available for an outcome in a meta-analysis. To account for the substantial chemical heterogeneity of herbal products, Petiveria alliacea preparations will be grouped a priori according to predefined criteria, extraction solvent and polarity (aqueous/polar versus organic/non-polar), plant part used, and whole-plant versus fractionated or standardized extract, and outcomes will be summarized separately within these predefined categories rather than pooled across them. Quantitative pooling will not be undertaken when studies differ in these core biological dimensions (different extract or solvent classes, plant parts, tumor lineages, or outcome definitions), even when statistical heterogeneity (𝐼2) appears acceptable, because pooling across biologically non-comparable conditions may generate misleading estimates. When a meta-analysis is not appropriate or feasible, the evidence will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline [15]. 3. Discussion This systematic review protocol describes a rigorous, pre-registered methodology to synthesize the antineoplastic evidence for Petiveria alliacea across experimental and clinical settings. To the best of the review team’s knowledge, this is the first systematic review with a prospectively registered protocol addressing this question, filling a recognized gap in the integrative oncology and phytomedicine literature. The global burden of cancer disproportionately affects low- and middle-income countries where plant-based medicines are widely used, justifying the systematic evaluation of ethnobotanically relevant plants with preclinical antineoplastic signals [1–3]. Petiveria alliacea is a compelling candidate: documented traditional use, partially characterized phytochemistry, and substantive preclinical data suggesting cytotoxic and immunomodulatory mechanisms [7,8]. The absence of a synthesized, critically appraised evidence base prevents rational prioritization of translational research or the development of evidence-based guidance for clinicians and regulators. The methodological strengths of this review include: a prospective PROSPERO registration, a comprehensive multi-database search across ten electronic databases, an independent dual screening with bibliographic blinding, a validated preclinical risk of bias, the use of reporting tools (SYRCLE, CAMARADES, and MDAR), and pre-specified subgroup analyses aligned with known sources of heterogeneity. The anticipated limitations of this work include publication bias toward positive results in preclinical oncology literature [13], heterogeneity in Petiveria alliacea preparations and cancer models, the restriction of eligible studies to three languages (English, Spanish, and Portuguese), which introduces a degree of language bias, and the probable paucity of clinical evidence. Conclusion As this is a protocol, no definitive conclusions can be drawn at this stage. The planned systematic review will provide a rigorous, comprehensive synthesis of the antineoplastic evidence for Petiveria alliacea across in vitro, in vivo, and clinical study designs, assessing the methodological quality of the existing literature, and generating specific recommendations for future research in integrative oncology. 5. The Itajaí-Açu watershed covers approximately 15,000 km², and, as Leite and Klein (1990) pointed out, the vegetation of this area is known to be very rich in tree species, lianas and epiphytes, especially for tree species such as canela-preta (Ocotea catharinensis Mez), laranjeirado-mato (Sloanea guianensis (Aubl.) Benth.), peroba (Aspidosperma australe Müll. Arg.) and tanheiro (Alchornea triplinervia (Spreng.) Müll. Arg.). Tree ferns dominates the understory like Alsophila setosa Kaulf., Cyathea phalerata Mart. and Cyathea corcovadensis (Raddi) Domin, besides the presence of shrubs of the genus Psychotria L. and Mollinedia Ruiz & Pavon (Sevegnani et al. 2013). Thus, the objective of this study was to characterize the floristic diversity of herbaceous and shrub species of the largest remnants of Atlantic Subtropical Rainforest in southern Brazil, the Parque Nacional da Serra do Itajaí. Materials and Methods Study Area The Parque Nacional da Serra do Itajaí (PNSI) was created in June 2004 with more than 57,000 ha. It is covered by Rainforest (Oliveira-Filho 2009), distributed in sub-montane, montane and upper montane secondary and primary vegetation. The region is predominantly mountainous with altitudes ranging from about 30 to 1000 m. Part of it, which belonged to the former Parque Natural Municipal Nascentes do Garcia, is located in Blumenau city, in the Middle Itajaí Valley, between the coordinates 27°06′ S and 49°10′ W, in Santa Catarina (Figure 1), southern Brazil. For logistics reasons, four locations were defined for field studies. The locations are: Parque Ecológico Spitzkopf, RPPN Buguerkopf, Morro do Sapo and Trilha da Chuva, all of them part of Parque Nacional da Serra do Itajaí. The PNSI is part of a major fragment of Atlantic Subtropical Rainforest, which has previously suffered from several human disturbances, but is now in an advanced stage of Introduction Santa Catarina’s flora is very well documented due to the memorable efforts of botanists such as Roberto Miguel Klein and Raulino Reitz, founders of Herbário Barbosa Rodrigues and Flora Ilustrada Catarinense authors. It is estimated that today 80% of the species are already published in the Flora Ilustrada Catarinense (Reitz 1965– 1989 and Reis 1999–2011), meaning 3,784 species in 929 genera and 159 families, published in 189 fascicles and 15,008 pages (Reis 2011). According to Flora do Brasil (2013), in Santa Catarina there are mentioned 4,434 angiosperm species (4,208 native), 420 ferns species latu sensu (415 native) and six gymnosperms (three native), totaling 4,860 taxa, which represents about 15% of all known plant species in Brazil and about 31% of the known species in the Atlantic rainforest (Stehmann et al. 2009). Despite of being recorded, many of these species have very few samples, often quite long time ago, particularly not arboreal species, which are often excluded from forest surveys. According to Feelei and Silman (2011), the more a species are collected, the better it can be evaluated for its conservation status, as well as decide appropriate strategies for their preservation. As pointed out by Gilliam and Roberts (2003), herbaceous synusiae is neglected because it does not represent the structure of the forest and also because it does not have commercial value, unlike the trees, which may have economic value assigned to the timber. However, native species often have useful properties, but lack studies prospects for them. The economic importance of herbs and shrubs is, for example, the major source of secondary compounds, widely studied searching for new drugs, besides providing food, fibers, industrial inputs, ornamental, essences, spices, among many other uses to humans (Mentz et al. 1997; Coradin et al. 2011). E-mail: luis_adriano_f@yahoo.com.br Abstract: This paper aim to characterize the herbaceous and shrub species diversity of Parque Nacional da Serra do Itajaí (PNSI). We identified 643 herbaceous and shrub species distributed in 110 families being the most representative family Asteraceae (62 species), Melastomataceae (49) and Rubiaceae (30), besides a two new records for Santa Catarina (Thelypteris glaziovii T.F. Reed and Pseudelephantopus spiralis Cronquist). We recorded 22 exotic species. Thus, due to the vast diversity of life and the rather large territory, PNSI is one of the most important spots for biodiversity conservation in Santa Catarina. DOI: 10.15560/10.6.1249

Rainfall are abundant and evenly distributed throughout the year, however, there is a period of more intense rain during the summer, with less than 60 days with less than 100 mm rainfall. The relative humidity is high, ranging from 84– 86% (Santa Catarina 1986). Data collection We collected fertile specimens by active search (Filgueiras et al.1994), in previously mentioned locations. One to three fertile individuals of each species were collected and, after processed, deposited at the Herbarium Dr. Roberto Michael Klein (FURB). When necessary, we collected sterile samples, and these were grown in a greenhouse until flowering. We identified the material searching in the literature, discussing with taxonomists and compared it to materials with other herbaria collections. Angiosperm species were classified according to the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group III (APG 2009), ferns according to Smith et al. (2006) and adaptations of Rothfels et al. (2012), Kramer and Green (1990) for Lycophytes and Christenhusz et al. (2011) for Gymnosperms. We compiled data published in Flora Ilustrada Catarinense (Reitz 1965), and herbariums FURB, FLOR, HBR, BHCB, CESJ, CNMT, CRI, FUEL, HEPH, HUCS, HVAT, ICN, JOI, LUSC, MBM, MFS, RB, UEC and UPCB through the CRIA database, aiming to increment the herbaceousshrub list species already sampled at PNSI. We considered in this study all vascular plants with a height equal to or less than 3 m that were using soil or rocks as substrate. We analyzed: species reported in the literature and collected species, new records for PNSI, new records for the state, exotic species, threatened species included at national and state red lists. We classified the PNSI species by life form according to Raunkiaer (1934). A collector curve (Figure 2) was generated to determine if the species are well sampled. Field trips were made over a half year, during the warm season (September to April), to collect the specimens in reproductive stage. Plants which were not determined at species level were excluded from analysis to avoid overestimating the number of species. Results We recorded 643 species from Parque Nacional da Ser­ ra do Itajaí (PNSI) (Table 1), these species were distributed in 486 (75.58%) Angiosperms with 86 families (78.18%); 145 (22.55%) fern species, with 21 families (21.81%); 11 species (1.71%) of Lycophytes into two families (1.9%) and one Gymnosperm (<1%). Reed (Thely­ pteridaceae) and Pseudelephantopus spiralis Cronquist (Asteraceae) is confirmed to be a new record for Santa Catarina state. From the 643 species recorded in this study, 22 were exotic species (Table 1). We also found five threatened species and a new species of Rhynchospora Vahl is been described. Discussion The importance of this Protected Areas for Atlantic Subtropical Rainforest (southern Brazil) biodiversity protection is proved, once again, by its richness. Adding up the tree species researched by the Management Plan of PNSI (Brasil 2009), where 340 tree and shrub species were recorded, as well as collections made by other researchers in PNSI, until now there were recorded 1,086 species of vascular. We found epiphytes species in herbaceous stratum, growing over the leaf litter layer on top of Morro do Sapo and Spitzkopf such as Prosthechea bulbosa (Vell.) W.E. Higgins, Prosthechea vespa (Vell.) W.E. Higgins and Coppensia flexuosa (Lodd.) Campacci (Orchidaceae), Vriesea erythrodactylon (E. Morren) E. Morren ex Mez, Vriesea rodigasiana E. Morren and Nidularium innocentii Lem. (Bromeliaceae), Pleiochiton blepharodes (DC.) Reginato et al. (Melastomataceae) and species of Nematanthus Schrad. (Gesneriaceae) as has already been reported by Klein (1980). The new record Thelypteris glaziovii had already been reported by Ponce (1998) in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul states, but no voucher was presented. Salino and Semir (2004) reduced its distribution only to southeastern Brazil, and more recently over a collection in Serra do Capivari, Campina Grande do Sul (Paraná), Schwartsburd and Xavier de Lima (2008) increased its distribution to Paraná state. Now we can confirm the reported made by Ponce (1998). Pseudelphantopus spiralis is a small ruderal herb, which a population of aproximated five individuals was found in a short stretch of the Spitzkopf’s trail. Is quoted by flora of Brazil with distribution in the states of Bahia, São Paulo and Acre. Possibly, as it is similar with ruderal species Elephantopus mollis, is poorly sampled. The 22 exotic species in PNSI, four ferns (Deparia petersenii (Kunze) M. Kato, Macrothelypteris torresiana (Gaudich.) Ching, Nephrolepis pectinata (Willd.) Schott. and Thelypteris dentata (Forssk.) E.P. St. John, which have already been registered by Gasper and Sevegnani (2010) and 17 angiosperms: Thunbergia alata Bojer ex Sims, Centella asiatica (L.) Urb., Bidens pilosa L., Galinsoga parviflora Cav., Tithonia diversifolia (Emsl.) A. Gray, Youngia japonica (L.) DC., Impatiens walleriana Hook.f., Cardamine bonariensis Juss. ex Pers, Drymaria cordata (L.) Willd. ex Schult., Stellaria media (L.) Vill., Tradescantia zebrina Bosse, Sechium edule (Jacq.) Sw., Psidium guajava L., Plantago major L., Eleusine indica (L.) Gaertn., Brugmansia suaveolens (Humb. & Bompl. ex Willd.) Bercht. & J. Presl, Pilea microphylla (L.) Liebm. and Hedichyum coronarium J.Koenig (Lista de Espécies da Flora do Brasil 2013; Schneider 2007). Most of these exotic species were found near Spitzkopf, where in the past, some areas were used for agriculture and cattle. Likely, intense visits in the other areas studied may explain the fact, since many exotic species are closely related to human presence, current or past (Wright 2005). In the tracks margins we found some important invasive species such as Impatiens walleriana and Hedichyum coronarium with dense populations close to watercourse. Five species in the PNSI are threatened, that is why we should consider important the conservation of this area. Two of these were already known by previous collections for PNSI, especially xaxim-bugio (Dicksonia sellowiana Hook.), as quoted by Gasper and Sevegnani (2010), classified as Critically Endangered (CR) in SC state and in Brazil as Vulnerable (VU), especially due to commercial exploitation (Windisch 2002). Heliconia farinosa Raddi (VU) is treated as threatened on the national list of IBAMA (2008), but apparently it is a common species in PNSI, often found in lowland areas, next to watercourses. Microlepia speluncae (L.T. Moore) was considered probably extinct (EX) in the state list of endangered species, but we found a small population in RPPN Bugerkopf. Piper ulei C. DC. (VU) was also found in a location close to a watercourse in Morro do Sapo, where there were some individuals, and finally, Vanilla dietschiana (Edwal) Garay. (VU) was found only once, an individual with several vegetative seedlings, from which a sample was collected in RPPN Bugerkopf. According to the samples curve, the number of species for PNSI is not stabilized, since it remained tilted, showing that the Parque Nacional da Serra do Itajaí is a extremely rich area, and 1,086 vascular plant species does not express its real richness. PNSI represents 0.6% of the state territory, yet its richness corresponds to nearly 22.6% of the total species described in Santa Catarina. Thus, we confirm the need for more research in the field in order to try to unravel the true biodiversity that this area hosts. The presence of three species categorized as threatened, and two new records for the state, besides a new species reinforces the importance of this area for the conservation of Atlantic Subtropical Rainforest remnants. On the other hand, the presence of exotic species points out this area vulnerability, especially in areas of strong human influence. Research Review Article Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences 87 (6): 711–26, June 2017/Article Diagnosis and management of soil fertility constraints in coconut (Cocos nucifera) : A review S K MALHOTRA1, H P MAHESWARAPPA2, V SELVAMANI3 and P CHOWDAPPA4 ICAR-Central Plantation Crops Research Institute, Kasaragod, Kerala 671 124 Received: 3 December 2016; Accepted: 5 March 2017 ABSTRACT Coconut (Cocos nucifera L.) is an important perennial plantation crop and to improve the productivity, the innate soil constraints should be ameliorated. The red, lateritic and sandy coconut soils are suffering with soil acidity, low CEC and poor nutrient reserve. A study on nutrient removal by coconut provides guidelines for the fertilizer input required. The effect of soil nutrient imbalance on the availability of nutrients emphasize the need based balanced fertilizer supply to coconut soils. The built up of soil available P in acidic red soils under continuous phosphatic fertilizer application strengthens the need to realize the soil test based fertilizer application. The potassium supply in the acid soils is poor, coconut being a huge feeder of potassium needs constant supply of potassium. Secondary and micronutrient deficiencies are emerging as potential yield limiting nutrients for coconut. Biomass recycling studies under coconut based cropping systems shows promising results in achieving the nutrient supply with the available biomass recycling through vermicompost. Minimizing the biomass exported out of farm especially coconut husk may improve potassium supply to palms through organic farming. Microbial studies showed that biomass recycling improved the beneficial microorganism in the rhizosphere and thereby enhances the nutrient availability. Fertigation technique showed higher nutrient use efficiency, soil and water conservation measures improved the yield of coconut in sandy soil and checks the losses through run-off and erosion in sloppy soils. Site specific soil management strategies can improve the coconut yield in an eco-friendly way. Key words: Biomass, Coconut, Fertigation, Nutrient management, Soil health, Vermicompost 3 The coconut palm (Cocos nucifera L.) globally cultivated in around 93 countries and in India, it is grown in 2.1 million ha (2015-16, 3rd estimates) with a production of 14 075 million nuts and an average productivity of 6 702 nuts/ha/year (CDB 2016). Coconut farming and allied activities provide livelihood security to millions of people in India. Hence, achieving and sustaining higher productivity and profitability from coconut farming is a paramount goal in serving this farming community. The price fluctuation, declining fertilizer response owing to the deteriorating soil health, increasing cost of fertilizers and lack of availability of organic manures are few of the major factors challenging to meet this goal. Understanding the nutrient removal, biomass availability, fertilizer/manure requirement, appropriate soil and moisture conservation measures, efficient methods of fertilizer application to improve nutrient use efficiency will enable to formulate soil nutrient management strategies towards improving and sustaining soil health in an ecofriendly way. Implementing these soil management strategies will be a way foreward in ensuring sustained higher coconut productivity and livelihood of coconut farmers. Soil requirement Red and lateritic and sandy soil types are the major soils in which the coconut is being cultivated. These are the soil types having naturally poor soil fertility status. On the other hand, coconut being a perennial crop with a lifespan of around 60 years and having simultaneously both vegetative and reproductive growth throughout the year, extracts more nutrients from the limited soil volume. Thereby, the soils which are having naturally poor nutrient reserve, loss their productivity potential very soon leading to the decline from the initial productivity of the plantations over the years if not properly manured. The ideal coconut growing soils are well drained and aerated with a minimum depth of 80 to 100 cm, pH range between 5 to near neutral, adequate nutrient availability and water holding capacity (Fremond 1964). The depth of the soil is one of the important soil physical criteria for the sustained productivity. Around 73% of roots of coconut are found within 2 m radius and most of them were confined to 31-120 cm depth (Kushwah et al. 1973). In middle aged palm, 96% of the roots present in 0-120 cm depth (Maheshwarappa et al. 2000). More number of main https://doi.org/10.56093/ijas.v87i6.70899

712 [Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences 87 (6) MALHOTRA ET AL. 4 and low organic carbon content, this soil type is subject to high leaching loses of applied nutrients during monsoon and severe moisture stress during summer. Improvement of the soil organic matter content is a pre-requisite for the successful management of coconuts on such soils. Hence, sustainable crop production could be achieved in this soil type through adoption of cropping systems approach along with soil moisture conservation methods. Fodder grass can be successfully grown as an intercrop in coconut gardens under coastal sandy soils by adopting appropriate soil moisture conservation measures. Incorporation of one layer of dried coconut husk in trenches and/or applying 5 cm thickness of coir pith in the planting zone significantly increases green and dry fodder yield due to higher soil moisture, nutrient availability especially potassium and enhanced biological activities in the rhizosphere when soil moisture conservation measures were implemented (Subramanian et al. 2007). Effect of soil compaction on the growth and activity of coconut roots in two soil series, namely, Andigama series (gravelly soil) and Madampe series (sandy loam soil) was studied by Vidhana Arachchi et al. (1999). The root activity in the Madampe series, with respect to moisture absorption was higher than that of the Andigama series due to low compaction of the former. Soil compaction higher than 250 N/cm2 restricted the activity of coconut roots in the gravelly soil. They also reported that high moisture extraction by coconut roots was confined to a depth ranging from 20 to 120 cm and of 20 to 250 cm in soils of Andigama and Madampe series, respectively, due to differences in soil compaction levels. Soil compaction limits the water absorption ability of coconut roots vertically from the base of the tree, rather than coconut root growth and penetration. Intercropping with Gliricidia sepium under coconut showed the possibility of improving degraded soil conditions of gravelly Andigama series which is having poor physical characters restricting palm growth and yield in intermediate zone of Sri Lanka. Coconut root growth also increased in A, AB and B horizons. These studies strongly suggested that Gliricidia sepium plays a major role in improving physical characters of infertile gravelly soils (Arachchi and Liyanage 1996). Soil acidity and salinity related constraints Soil acidity: Almost all red and lateritic soils under coconut, which are formed under humid tropical conditions, have A13+ as the dominant cation, and hence, their pH is very low (4.2-5.8). The high Al and Fe revert the soluble phosphates into insoluble ones. The soil acidity can be managed by applying liming material based on the lime requirement of the soil. For acid sulphate soils, suppression of aluminium could be achieved only by using magnesium silicate. This facilitates inactivation of Al as aluminum silicate and the magnesium sulphate thus formed can be leached out of the system. According to Nambiar et al. (1975), the application of seaweed as manure reduce the acidity to a certain extent. Soil salinity: In low lying areas where the soils are frequently inundated by sea water or submerged with roots was found in layer of 31-60 cm depth and decreases in the deeper layers (61-90 and 91-120 cm) (Dhanapal et al. 2000). Hence, a minimum depth of one meter soil is a pre-requisite for planting coconut which gives a good physical support and better anchorage against gusts of winds (Ganarajah 1953). A minimum depth of 80 to 100 cm was observed as ideal by Fremond (1964). The soil physical constrains like hard soil pan, bed rock or permanent water table within one metre depth are unsuitable for coconut. Coconut palm adapts to a wide range of soil acidity. The ideal soil pH for coconut growing soils ranges between 5 to near neutral (Fremond 1964). The pH of representative Indian soils is reported to be in the range of 5.2 to 8.0 (Menon and Nair 1952). Coconut can be cultivated in the soil pH range of 5 to 8 (Manciot et al.1979). Coconut being a semi-halophytic plant can tolerate soil salinity up to 0.6% which is beyond tolerable limits to many other crops. Hence, the total soluble salts in the soil are not a serious problem for coconut cultivation (Sankaranarayanan et al. 1958). Coconut responds very well to judicious fertilizer application and irrigation. Therefore with appropriate management, coconut can be grown even on the poorest soils with good soil drainage and aeration in sub-soil. Since, coconut is grown in the tropical condition most of the soils are deficient in the organic matter except the soils of the humid tropics like lateritic soil of the hilly region and the alluvial soils. Manciot et al. (1979) suggested a threshold value of 1.0% organic carbon for coconut soils. The soil nitrogen supply is directly related to the soil organic fractions whereas, soil phosphorus level does not pose a serious problem to coconut cultivation and adequate potassium supply must be ensured for higher coconut productivity. Among the secondary and micronutrients, supply of magnesium, sulphur, boron and zinc are very important since they are generally in short supply in many of the coconut growing tropical soils. SOIL CONSTRAINTS AND MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES In India, coconut is mainly grown in laterite and lateritic, coastal sand, red sandy loam, coral and alluvial soils. These soils come mainly under four soil orders viz., Alfisols, Entisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols. These are mainly acidic in nature with low fertility status and suffer from varying degree of nutrient/moisture stress. Physical constraints Coconut grown under coastal sandy soil without manuring results in lower yield due to poor physicochemical characters viz., high bulk density, poor aggregate stability, poor water holding capacity, high soil temperature and poor soil fertility status (Srinivasa Reddy and Upadhyay 2002). Even regular application of chemical fertilizers failed in building up of soil nutrient status in littoral sandy soil mainly due to low nutrient retention capacity of the soil (Srinivasa Reddy et al. 1999). The very low clay content leads to high infiltration and percolation rate coupled with low CEC

Potash was found to be removed most, followed by nitrogen, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. The quantity of nutrients removed varies with the soil type and yield. Palms growing on coastal alluvium removed 70 kg K2O/ha but the average removal from red sandy loam and laterite was around 53 kg K2O/ha (Ramanandan and George 1982). Variation in the capacity of nutrient removal pattern depending upon targeted yield has been documented in horticultural crops including plantation crops. Removal of K from soil was observed to be 3-4 times higher in perennial crops than N and P compared to annual crops. Hence, nutrient removal patterns uphold two cardinal points, one in many crops magnitude of removal of K is higher than N or P and two that highlight towards necessity of tailoring fertilizer requirement as per crop. In a study made in India, considering the nutrient removal rate projections, in the year of 2016-17, the fertilizer requirement for horticulture crops will be 7.56 million tonnes (Malhotra and Srivastava 2015). Nutrient management Long-term studies have indicated that cultural practices alone are superior to no cultivation and no manuring. Cultural practices alone, like cultivation of interspaces twice a year and weed control using herbicides produced poor yields ranging from 10.7 to 32.3 nuts/palm/year as compared to fertilizer treatments coupled with cultural practices which produced yields ranging from 83-107.9 nuts/palm/year, indicating that cultural practices alone could not sustain higher productivity. Soil and leaf analysis of palms under different cultural and fertilizer treatments strongly suggests that for satisfactory growth and productivity of palms in the red sandy loam soil mere cultural treatments alone cannot improve the nutritional status of palms and supplementing the nutrition with inorganic fertilizer and organic manures is necessary to sustain productivity (Khan et al. 1996). Fertilizer management technologies have been developed for different horticulture crops in the different countries and provinces based on scientific principles (Srivastava and Malhotra 2014, Meena et al. 2006, Aishwath and Malhotra 2013). Optimum requirement of fertilizers for different fruits and vegetable crops have been worked out by different workers and described in the review (Malhotra and Srivastava 2015). Inorganic and organic fertilizer can be found in different types of products like compound, straight, controlled released, blended, granulated, water soluble and liquid fertilizer (Malhotra 2016, Srivastava et al. 2014, 2015). The liquid fertilizers, as special class of fertilizers provide an enormous possibility of tailoring nutrient use across critical growth stages, a pre-requisite for better nutrient-use-efficiency. Customized fertilization/ fertigation is another potential reality, besides its suitability in site specific nutrient managements. In this background, these issues have been addressed in the review (Malhotra, 2016). brackish water during certain seasons of the year, the resulted excess salinity may create some production problems. Drainage facilities and check bunds can reduce the inundation. Coconut cultivated in non-traditional saline/alkaline areas face considerable limitation due to the dominance of sodium, carbonates and bicarbonates. Application of more organic matter in the planting pits along with soil-sand mixture in equal amounts also observed to reduce the salt problems. Soil fertility constraints Generally, the sandy soils contain very low amount of soil nitrogen and leaching loss of nitrate is very high in sandy soil followed by sandy loam and red soils. The available phosphorus status of 15 soil series and four soil orders (Ultisol, Entisol, Alfisol and Oxisol) in the major coconut-growing regions of Sri Lanka were found to be very low in almost all soils except some of the sandy soils (Entisols) which had marginal to moderate P content (Loganathan et al.1984). Liming and calcium containing phosphatic fertilizers can meet the calcium requirement in highly acidic soil. The availability of Ca in coral soils is very high and often antogonise the uptake of K, Mg and Na by coconut. In India, both magnesium and sulphur are either deficient or tending towards deficiency in most of the soils in Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra and North Eastern States of India. The deficiency of sulphur was reported from Papua and New Guinea (Southern 1969) and some of the East African and South East Asian countries (Ollagnier and Ochs 1972). The concentrations of copper and zinc are low in black and coral soils. Boron deficiency is emerging in most of the laterite, red, alluvial and coastal sandy soils in the humid tropics. SOIL HEALTH MANAGEMENT Nutrient requirement Quantification of nutrient exhaust usually provides useful guidelines for optimizing the quantity of the individual nutrients and their proportion in which they have to be applied to sustain the soil fertility and coconut productivity. The nutrient exhaust, studies showed that the proportionate requirement of NPK of the palm in terms of N, P2O5, K2O is 02:1:3. The quantitative order of requirement of major nutrients for adult bearing palm is K>N>Ca>Mg>P. Potassium dominates the nutrient requirement of the palm while P requirement is found to be the least (Pillai and Davis 1963, Ramadasan and Lal 1966). The annual exhaust computed from one hectare of 173 palms in sandy loam soil is 65.6, 29.7, 84.5, 47.4 and 20.3 kg of N, P2O5, CaO and MgO, respectively, taking into account the nuts, fallen leaves spathes and the stem growth (Pillai and Davis 1963). The amounts of macronutrients lost through the removal of plant components from the field of Typica × Typica coconut palms yielding an average of 17, 38 nuts/ha/year in Sri Lanka, were 116.79 kg N, 14.02 kg P, 245.43 kg K, 40.47 kg Ca, and 33.66 kg Mg/

714 [Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences 87 (6) 6 respectively (Wahid et al. 1988). Potassium adsorption studies in a red sandy loam soil (Arenic Paleustult) under various fertilizer regimes in coconut under coconut based cropping system at Kasaragod revealed that the optimum K application to maximize the soil solution K for optimum plant nutrition ranged from 662 ppm (full dose) to 692 ppm (no fertilizer) (Upadhyay et al. 2005). The potassium supply can be regulated in sandy soil by suitable management practices. Higher build up of available potassium in littoral beach sandy soil was observed when inorganic fertilizers were applied with different organics. Maximum build up was obtained when potassium was applied along with coconut pith (Nambiar et al. 1983). Bopaiah et al. (1998) studied the effect of slow release N and P fertilizers (different combinations of urea, urea formaldehyde, neem coated urea, lac coated urea mixed along with coir dust, tar, single super phosphate, mussorie rock phosphate and muriate of potash) Among the slow release N fertilizers ureaform, neem cake coated urea and coir dust mixed with urea have been found to remain for a long period in the sandy soil, thus facilitating availability of N in the more permeable soil. Mussorie phosphate is equally efficient as super phosphate in sandy soil. A long-term experiment conducted Kasaragod in littoral sandy soil indicated that annual application of fertilizers for a period of 32 years to coconut resulted in a marked increase in the available phosphorus and potassium status in soil, but a marginal change in soil available nitrogen status. The yield of coconut increased with the higher levels of nutrient application, and the highest yield was recorded in the treatment of 1000:437:1667g of N, P, K/palm/yr (Srinivasa Reddy et al. 2001). The Mitscherlich-Bray model is popularly used in most of the field crops. This principle was employed to evaluate the nutrient requirement of three high yielding genotoypes of coconut by Khan et al. (1986). They indicated that the nutrient requirement of D × T hybrid was relatively lower than that of Talls to produce the same quantity of yield. Tall × Dwarf hybrid behaved intermediate between D x T and WCT. They further evaluated the efficiency of soil and fertilizer nutrients with respect to productivity. It is also possible to forecast coconut productivity for a given quantity of nutrient inputs. The application of fertilizers through drip fertigation resulted in a marked increase in available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium status in soil. Coconut yield was significantly higher in 100% NPK fertigation (131 nuts/palm/year) which was on par with 75 and 50% NPK applied through drip irrigation. Hence, through fertigation 50% saving of chemical fertilizers is possible which ensures the higher efficiency of nutrients in crop production (Subramanian et al. 2012). A study on the effect of fertigation on the productivity of coconut was conducted at Horticulture Research Station, Arsikere (Karnataka).
