Multivariate analysis methodology (PCA and HCA) The chemical composition data of Siparuna guianensis (Aubl.), compiled from different studies reported in the literature, were organized into a data matrix in which rows represented the samples and columns corresponded to the identiﬁed chemical constituents, expressed as relative percentage (%). Only compounds reported in the selected studies were included in the multivariate analysis. Prior to the statistical analyses, the data were subjected to autoscaling standardization (mean-centered and variance-scaled to unit variance) in order to eliminate the inﬂuence of differences in variable magnitude and to ensure an equivalent contribution of all chemical constituents. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied as an exploratory method to reduce data dimensionality and to identify patterns of similarity and variability among samples, considering variations associated with different years of collection and reported chemical proﬁles. The principal components were selected based on eigenvalues greater than 1 (Kaiser criterion) and cumulative explained variance, with emphasis on those components accounting for the largest proportion of the total variance. The PCA results were interpreted using score plots, which allowed visualization of sample distribution and grouping, and loading plots, which were used to identify the chemical compounds most responsible for sample discrimination. Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) was performed as a complementary technique to PCA in order to assess the similarity among samples and to conﬁrm the clustering patterns observed. Euclidean distance as the dissimilarity measure and the complete linkage method as the clustering criterion. The results were expressed as dendrograms, allowing visualization of similarity relationships among samples and identiﬁcation of groups with similar chemical proﬁles. All statistical analyses were carried out using Minitab version 22 (free version), adopting an exploratory approach suitable for review studies based on secondary data obtained from different bibliographic sources. Literature review After bibliometric ﬁltering and article selection, additionally, the synonyms of the species’ scientiﬁc name were veriﬁed using informations from the following online databases: (Plants of the World Online) ‘‘The Plant List’’, ‘‘World Flora Online’’ and ‘‘Flora do Brasil’’ (Peixoto 2026), which identiﬁed the following synonyms for the species: ‘‘Siparuna discolor’’; ‘‘Siparuna panamensis’’; ‘‘Angelina divergentifolia’’; ‘‘Citrosma camporum’’; ‘‘Citrosma discolor’’; ‘‘Citrosma guianensis’’; ‘‘Citrosma guianensis f. divergentifolia’’; ‘‘Citrosma guianensis f. nuda’’; ‘‘Citrosma guianensis f. nuda’’; ‘‘Citrosma oligocarpa’’; ‘‘Siparuna foetida’’; ‘‘Siparuna guianensis var. divergentifolia’’; ‘‘Siparuna guianensis var. glabrescens’’; ‘‘Siparuna guianensis var. longifo´lia’’; ‘‘Siparuna guianensis var. nitens’’; ‘‘Siparuna savanicola’’; ‘‘Siparuna archeri’’; ‘‘Siparuna arianeae’’; ‘‘Siparuna cavalcantei’’; ‘‘Siparuna duckeana’’; ‘‘Siparuna itacaiunensis’’; ‘‘Citriosma guianensis’’; ‘‘Citrosma guianensis var. nuda’’;‘‘Siparuna camporum’’. A narrative literature review was then conducted to integrate and contextualize the experimental evidence regarding the essential oil of S. guianensis, with primary emphasis on reported biological activities. The full texts of all included articles were carefully examined, focusing on chemical composition, major constituents, and biological activity. Results and discussion Bibliometric results The search strategy applied in WoS-CC retrieved 74 documents related to Siparuna guianensis. After applying the predeﬁned inclusion criteria, 25 articles were selected for detailed qualitative and quantitative evaluation. This marked reduction indicates that, although S. guianensis has been extensively investigated from botanical and phytochemical perspectives, only approximately 34% of the available literature establishes a direct association between volatile composition and biological function. This ﬁnding reveals a fragmented research landscape characterized by abundant chemical proﬁling but comparatively limited bioprospecting of biological activities. The earliest and most cited study was published in 2013 and investigated the chemical composition and antioxidant properties of S. guianensis essential oil; however, no antioxidant activity was detected (Andrade et al. 2013). In contrast, the most recent publication (2025) employed an integrated approach combining phytochemical characterization, in silico molecular docking, and in vitro bioassays to demonstrate larvicidal activity, highlighting acetylcholinesterase inhibition as a potential mechanism of action (Montan˜o-Campaz et al. 2025) (Table 1). The analysis of the selected articles indicates that research on S. guianensis essential oil is predominantly centered on insecticidal and vector-control applications, particularly against Aedes aegypti and agricultural pests, which also account for the most highly cited publications. In contrast, studies approaching antimicrobial, antioxidant, antiparasitic, or antiviral activities generally exhibit lower citation impact and often report only moderate efﬁcacy which highlights the peripheral role of S. guianensis in these research domains. Phytochemical data reveal pronounced intraspeciﬁc variability, with b-myrcene, a-bisabolol, spathulenol, curzerenone, germacrene D, c-elemene, and shyobunone derivatives emerging as recurrent major constituents (a comprehensive phytochemical characterization is addressed in Sect. ‘‘Chemical compositions Siparuna guianensis’’). Biological activity appears to be strongly chemotype-dependent, as evidenced by studies demonstrating superior acaricidal and anthelmintic effects in a-bisabolol-rich oils and consistent insecticidal performance in b-myrcene, dominant proﬁles. More recent investigations increasingly integrate molecular docking, enzyme inhibition assays, and membrane permeability studies, providing more sophisticated biological assays. This modular organization favors repeated chemical characterization of similar chemotypes across independent studies, while hindering the development of uniﬁed chemometric frameworks and standardized biological protocols. In contrast, keywords related to mammalian pharmacology or central nervous system outcomes were notably absent, while antioxidant and antitumoral themes appeared only sporadically. According to Zipf’s Law, the most frequently occurring keywords tend to represent the conceptual core of a research domain. In our present analysis, the predominance of chemically oriented terms conﬁrms that investigations of Siparuna guianensis essential oil remain largely anchored in phytochemical proﬁling instead of mechanistic biological exploration. To assess the global distribution of research on S. guianensis essential oil and its biological activities, the countries of corresponding authors were analyzed (Fig. 5). This pronounced geographic concentration reﬂects both biological and structural factors. As S. guianensis is native to South America (i.e., particularly Brazil), local access to plant material likely facilitates experimental investigation. Moreover, South American biomes, especially the Amazon, represent one of the world’s richest reservoirs of biodiversity and bioactive natural products, encouraging regionally driven phytochemical and pharmacological research. Despite increasing globalization in science, studies on endemic species often remain geographically localized. The dominance of Brazilian research may therefore be attributed not only to species availability but also to the presence of established research groups specializing in medicinal plants and essential oils. Based on the compiled studies, Andrade (2013, 2016), Aguiar (2015), Melo (2017), Ferreira (2017, 2019, 2020), Lourenc¸o (2018-Gurupi 1,Gurupi 2 and Formoso do Araguaia), Arruda (2019), Santana de Oliveira et al., (2020), Moura et al. (2024-SG1 to SG6), it is possible to identify structured chemical patterns involving different groups of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes, reﬂecting the metabolic plasticity of the species (Table 3). The study conducted by Andrade (Andrade et al. 2013) reported a proﬁle dominated by bicyclogermacrene (16.71%) and b-myrcene (13.14%), accompanied by relevant amounts of germacrene D (8.68%) and other sesquiterpenes. The results from Aguiar (2015) expand this perspective by demonstrating clear tissue-speciﬁc metabolism. In this study, leaves, stems (branches), and fruits were analyzed separately, resulting in distinct chemical proﬁles. The leaves were characterized by a marked predominance of bmyrcene (79.71%), whereas stems and fruits showed substantial amounts of germacrene D (9-9.4%) and 2-undecanone (12-26%). These patterns indicate that tissue differentiation signiﬁcantly modulates terpenoid biosynthesis, reinforcing the inﬂuence of organ-speciﬁc metabolic pathways and functional roles. The predominance of monoterpenes, especially bmyrcene, has been further supported by studies such as Melo (2017) (45.62%), Lourenc¸o (2018-Gurupi 1,Gurupi 2, and Formoso do Araguaia, * 70-81%), and Ferreira (2019) (48.59%). These ﬁndings suggest that populations from regions with warmer climates and higher irradiance, such as Tocantins, Para´, and Maranha˜o, tend to synthesize elevated proportions of hydrocarbon monoterpenes. Similar patterns were reported by Diniz (2022-VI: 79.47%) and (Santos et al. 2023) indicating that b-myrcene constitutes a recurrent chemical feature in several Amazonian chemotypes. In contrast, other studies reported a dominance of hydrocarbon and oxygenated sesquiterpenes, forming a second chemical group within the species. Germacrene D appears above 10% in Aguiar (Aguiar et al. 2015), (Andrade et al. 2016), (Ferreira et al. 2017), (Arruda et al. 2019), (Santana de Oliveira et al. 2020), Ferreira (Ferreira et al. 2020), and Moura et al. (2020), with even higher values observed in Diniz (2022-TO: 25%; VI: 31.9%). These data suggest that germacrene D is associated with chemotypes enriched in sesquiterpenes, potentially inﬂuenced by environmental conditions such as clay-rich soils, shaded habitats, and elevated relative humidity. Bicyclogermacrene, another relevant marker, was a major constituent in Andrade (Andrade et al. 2013), Aguiar (Aguiar et al. 2015), Lourenc¸o (2018), and speciﬁc proﬁles described by Santos et al. Statistical analyses The multivariate analysis based on principal component analysis (PCA) reveals a structured chemical variation across the essential oil samples, with the ﬁrst two principal components (PC1 and PC2) serving as the main axes describing compositional differentiation (Fig. 6). PC1 accounts for 13.0% of the total variance (eigenvalue = 19.402), whereas PC2 explains an additional 9.2% (eigenvalue = 13.723), resulting in a cumulative variance of 22.2%. Although the explained variance may appear modest, this is expected given the high dimensionality of the dataset (149 variables) and the compositional complexity typical of essential oils, which frequently comprise numerous low-abundance constituents. Importantly, despite the distributed variance, PC1 and PC2 effectively capture the major chemical trends and reveal clear chemotypic structuring rather than random dispersion. The distribution of samples across the PCA score space demonstrates distinct compositional groupings rather than a continuous gradient, indicating the presence of differentiated chemotypes (Fig. 6). The chemical separation along PC1 primarily reﬂects a Fig. 3 Authorship landscape of Siparuna guianensis essential oil research: A global co-authorship network; B leading author collaboration network; C top authors ranked by publication count; D authors ranked by total citations; and E corresponding authorship distribution among the most proliﬁc contributors 123 Phytochem Rev (2026) 25:5405–5446 5419

Samples positioned in the positive region of PC1 are predominantly characterized by higher relative abundances of monoterpene hydrocarbons and oxygenated monoterpenes, including b-myrcene, camphene, (E)- b-ocimene, and limonene. Conversely, samples located toward the negative side of PC1 are strongly associated with elevated proportions of sesquiterpene hydrocarbons and oxygenated sesquiterpenes. This trend demonstrates that PC1 effectively functions as a chemical axis discriminating lighter, more volatile monoterpene fractions from heavier, more structurally complex sesquiterpene components. The loading structure associated with PC1 further reinforces this interpretation (Fig. 7). The compounds exhibiting the strongest negative contributions to PC1 include sesquiterpene hydrocarbons (a-ylangene, agurjunene, cis-muurola-3,5-diene, trans-cadina-1,4diene, b-ylangene, b-selinene) and oxygenated sesquiterpenes (germacrone, trans-muurola-4(14),5diene). In contrast, positive contributions to PC1 are primarily associated with monoterpene constituents such as b-myrcene, camphene, (E)-b-ocimene, and limonene. Although the magnitude of these positive loadings is lower compared to the dominant sesquiterpene contributors, their combined inﬂuence clearly distinguishes samples enriched in monoterpene hydrocarbons from those dominated by sesquiterpenes. indicating substantial chemical divergence relative to the core groups. These late-joining samples are characterized by either reduced sesquiterpene content or elevated levels of monoterpenes and oxygenated constituents, consistent with their separation along the positive side of PC1 in the PCA. This pattern indicates that chemical differentiation is not uniform across the dataset and that certain samples deviate signiﬁcantly from the dominant sesquiterpene-rich chemotype. The overall structure of the dendrogram reveals at least two major chemical lineages: one deﬁned by sesquiterpene-rich compositions dominated by germacrane-, ylangane-, and muurolane-type skeletons (exempliﬁed by Cluster 2), and another characterized by higher proportions of monoterpenes and oxygenated compounds. The alignment of these clusters with the PCA loading structure reinforces the interpretation that these groupings reﬂect meaningful biochemical differentiation rather than statistical artifact. Collectively, the HCA results indicate that while a subset of samples forms highly cohesive clusters with strong chemical similarity (notably R2, R8, R9, and R12 in Cluster 2), other samples display marked divergence, resulting in a structured but heterogeneous compositional landscape. The dominant role of sesquiterpenes in deﬁning cluster boundaries highlights the importance of these compounds as chemotaxonomic markers within the dataset, while the variable distribution of monoterpenes and oxygenated constituents contributes to ﬁner-scale differentiation among samples. The convergence of PCA and HCA results provides strong evidence for distinct chemotypic organization within the dataset. The primary axis of variation captured by PC1, deﬁned by the balance between sesquiterpene-dominated and monoterpene-dominated proﬁles, aligns closely with the cluster groupings observed in the dendrogram. This concordance indicates that the multivariate structure is chemically meaningful and reﬂects underlying compositional gradients rather than statistical artifact. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the essential oil proﬁles exhibit discrete compositional structuring, supporting the identiﬁcation of distinct chemotypes and reinforcing the value of multivariate approaches for resolving complex phytochemical datasets. Antioxidant potential Due to the high chemical variability of EOs, it is common to evaluate their speciﬁc antioxidant activities, which, even within the same species, may vary depending on their major chemical constituents; moreover, the different methods used to assess antioxidant activity in biological systems are relatively fast, simple, and inexpensive, which justiﬁes their application in phytochemical studies (Huang et al. 2025). Among the selected studies, all were conducted in Brazil, and the most commonly used method was the quantitative 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical scavenging assay, one of the most widely applied free radical scavenging assays according to the literature; in addition, the second most frequently used method was the lipid peroxidation assay based on the b-carotene/linoleic acid cooxidation method (Mendonc¸a et al. 2022). biological activity potential Repellent and insecticidal activity The essential oil of Siparuna guianensis has attracted considerable pharmacological interest; however, an important aspect to be highlighted in this review is its potent activity against insect vectors and agricultural pests (Ferreira et al. 2019). Among the biological properties most consistently reported, insecticidal and repellent activities are the most frequently investigated, reﬂecting the growing body of research focused on this ﬁeld. This increasing interest is supported by experimental evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of this species against agricultural pests as well as mosquitoes of medical importance, underscoring its potential for further exploration in vector control and pest management strategies (Aguiar et al. 2015; Ferreira et al. 2017; Ferreira et al. 2019; Montan˜oCampaz et al. 2025). An important study highlighted in this section investigated the potential of nanoemulsiﬁcation of S. guianensis essential oil against mosquito vectors of dengue, Zika, and chikungunya viruses. The results showed that this formulation strategy substantially enhanced larvicidal activity compared to the nonformulated oil, demonstrating that appropriate delivery systems can signiﬁcantly improve bioefﬁcacy (Ferreira et al. 2019). In line with these ﬁndings, encapsulation of S. guianensis essential oil in chitosan nanoparticles prolonged its residual mosquitocidal activity against Aedes aegypti and maintained larvicidal effectiveness over time, indicating that nanostructured carriers can modulate release kinetics and protect volatile phytochemicals from rapid degradation (Ferreira et al. 2020). Additional investigations have also demonstrated insecticidal and repellent activity of the oil against Culex quinquefasciatus, another urban mosquito vector of epidemiological relevance, reinforcing the broad applicability of this species in mosquito control strategies (Aguiar et al. 2015). In addition to its notable activity against mosquito larvae, the insecticidal spectrum of S. guianensis essential oil extends to insects of major agricultural and economic importance. A study evaluating this oil demonstrated activity against wax moth species (Galleria mellonella and Achroia grisella), pests commonly associated with beekeeping, while also showing selective toxicity with reduced adverse effects on honey bees (Apis mellifera), a crucial nontarget pollinator (Ferreira et al. 2017). This broader spectrum of activity highlights the versatility of S. guianensis essential oil within integrated pest management frameworks. Another reported activity involves beetles such as Tribolium castaneum, an important pest of stored grains. The study indicated that essential oils from Neotropical plant species, including S. guianensis, may be applicable for the control of this type of agricultural pest (Pino-Benitez et al. 2024), highlighting the relevance of research exploring the potential of essential oils as botanical insecticides. In addition to investigating direct toxicity, some studies have explored the repellent capacity of the essential oil associated with the reduction of hostseeking and oviposition behavior in insects, particularly mosquitoes. This deterrent effect is associated with the volatile terpenoid proﬁle characteristic of the genus, rich in monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes that interfere with the olfactory and neurobehavioral pathways of insects (Aguiar et al. 2015; Montan˜oCampaz et al. 2025). Beyond direct toxicity, the repellent properties of S. guianensis essential oil have been implicated in reducing insect host-seeking and oviposition behaviors, particularly in mosquito species. Experimental studies evaluating both insecticidal and behavioral endpoints support a deterrent effect associated with the volatile terpenoid proﬁle characteristic of the genus, which is rich in monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes known to interfere with insect olfactory and neurobehavioral pathways (Aguiar et al. 2015; Montan˜o-Campaz et al. 2025). Importantly, the integration of formulation technologies such as nanoemulsions, biopolymeric nanoparticles, and starch-based microparticles has been shown to enhance the insecticidal performance of S. guianensis essential oil while potentially improving its environmental compatibility. Encapsulation approaches using biodegradable matrices can increase stability, modulate release, and prolong biological activity, helping to overcome common limitations of essential oils, such as volatility and rapid degradation under ﬁeld conditions. Overall, the available experimental evidence indicates that the essential oil of S. guianensis represents a promising bioactive resource with insecticidal and repellent potential against urban vectors, agricultural 123 5438 Phytochem Rev (2026) 25:5405–5446

pests, and storage insects, supporting further research that integrates phytochemical characterization, advanced delivery systems, ecological safety, and resistance-management perspectives toward the development of sustainable pest and vector control strategies. Antimicrobial activity Essential oils are volatile compounds that are primarily synthesized as secondary metabolites of glucose metabolism in plants and are mostly obtained through processes such as hydrodistillation or steam distillation from various plant structures. The essential oil of S. guianensis contains sesquiterpenes, oxygenated sesquiterpenes, and monoterpene hydrocarbons, which predominantly exhibit hydrophobic characteristics (Santana de Oliveira et al. 2020). Gram-negative bacteria possess an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides (LPS), which confers a hydrophilic surface; therefore, hydrophobic compounds are generally unable to cross these intact membranes (Cox et al. 2001). A study conducted by Andrade et al. (Andrade et al. 2015) demonstrated that S. guianensis essential oil exhibited inhibitory effects against Gram-positive bacteria such as Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus but showed no inhibitory activity against Gram-negative bacteria. The compound apinene showed the highest biological activity against L. monocytogenes. In addition, S. guianensis essential oil demonstrated strong antifungal activity, with lower inhibitory concentrations against Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, Trichophyton rubrum, and Aspergillus fumigatus. Santana de Oliveira et al., (2020) investigated the essential oil of S. guianensis and identiﬁed trans-belemenone and atractylone as the most abundant compounds in the sample. Molecular docking studies revealed positive interactions with target proteins, such as Candida albicans N-myristoyltransferase and Escherichia coli enoyl reductase. The predominance of hydrophobic interactions suggests that the ligand exhibits good complementarity with the active sites of the enzymes studied, which may contribute to increased complex stability and potential biological activity. In this context, the low RMSD values, combined with favorable energetic contributions obtained by the MM/GBSA method, reinforce the stability of the formed complexes and suggest good potential of the ligand as an inhibitor of the evaluated target proteins. The essential oil of S. guianensis also demonstrated inhibitory activity against Rhizoctonia solani, as well as inhibition of mycelial growth of Sclerotium rolfsii. In this study, the major components identiﬁed were the monoterpene b-myrcene and 2-undecanone (Arruda et al. 2019). De Jesus et al. (de Jesus et al. 2020) conducted a study to evaluate the use of essential oils as a therapeutic alternative for foodborne diseases. Compared to other oils analyzed, S. guianensis did not demonstrate antimicrobial activity against E. coli strains; however, it exhibited activity against Staphylococcus spp., including a multidrug-resistant strain, although this was not the most pronounced result of the study. In a study by Melo et al. (Melo et al. 2017), the most abundant compounds identiﬁed were the acyclic monoterpene b-myrcene and the sesquiterpenes germacrene D and (E, E)-farnesol. The essential oil showed antibacterial efﬁcacy against Streptococcus mutans strains. The same study also evaluated anticariogenic activity, which was evidenced by activity against S. sobrinus and S. mutans, in addition to antimycobacterial activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, M. kansasii, and M. avium. These effects were directly associated with the presence of viridiﬂorol compounds in the essential oil (Melo et al. 2017). Moura et al. (2020) investigated the essential oil of S. guianensis, whose composition was mainly characterized by b-myrcene, germacrene D, and espicurzerenone. Antimicrobial activity was observed against E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus. Even at low concentrations, inhibition of bacterial growth was observed, while higher concentrations completely inhibited growth. Additionally, the essential oil increased cellular potassium efﬂux. Nucleotide leakage was also observed following exposure to the essential oil, and the authors demonstrated that none of the concentrations tested caused toxicity to human monocytic cells (TPH1). The results obtained in this study indicate the potential efﬁcacy of the essential oil of Siparuna guianensis, particularly when compared with data reported for essential oils from other species or genera (da Costa et al. 2024; Ferreira et al. 2025). When compared to a reference antibiotic, the essential 123 Phytochem Rev (2026) 25:5405–5446 5439

oil exhibited a greater ability to alter bacterial membrane permeability, as evidenced by increased K? efﬂux. Molecular docking analyses suggest that compounds present in the essential oil, particularly germacrene B, exhibit high afﬁnity for active regions of bacterial DNA and RNA polymerases, potentially inducing conformational changes capable of inhibiting replication and transcription processes (Robinson and Oijen 2013). The bacteriostatic or bactericidal effect of S. guianensis essential oil may be explained by the inhibition of microbial growth due to damage to membrane integrity caused by lipophilic components present in the oil, leading to loss of cellular pH homeostasis and inorganic ions (Melo et al. 2017; Santana de Oliveira et al. 2020). Furthermore, increased potassium ion efﬂux and nucleotide leakage suggest that the essential oil compromises the integrity of the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, allowing the release of essential intracellular components (Roosild et al. 2010; Bajpai et al. 2013). Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the phytochemical composition of S. guianensis essential oil is dependent on seasonality and collection site, resulting in variation of major and minor compounds. Overall, the ﬁndings indicate that Gram-positive bacteria are more sensitive to the effects of the essential oil, likely due to the volatile compounds present in its composition. Antiparasitic activity Few studies have demonstrated the activity of S. guianensis against intracellular protozoa. In an in vitro analysis, the ethanolic extract, ethyl acetate fraction, aqueous fraction, volatile oil, and isolated a-bisabolol from S. guianensis Aubl. showed activity against the RH2F1 strain of Toxoplasma gondii in ﬁbroblasts (Souza et al. 2021). After parasite infection, the fractions exhibited partial modulation of intracellular proliferation. When used as a pretreatment, the ethanolic extract and the ethyl acetate fraction directly inhibited the parasite (Souza et al. 2021). The essential oils obtained from the leaves of different chemotypes of S. guianensis, rich in abisabolol and germacrene D, demonstrated acaricidal activity against Rhipicephalus microplus. In larval proliferation assays, samples containing a-bisabolol exhibited a 100% mortality rate, although all essential oils caused high mortality in R. microplus. In addition, a-bisabolol–rich samples showed a reduction in both the number and viability of eggs (Diniz et al. 2022). Anthelmintic properties were evaluated for the ethanolic extract, essential oil, aqueous and ethyl acetate fractions of S. guianensis, as well as for the compound a-bisabolol, against eggs of Strongyloides venezuelensis. In larval motility and egg hatching assays, all samples exhibited ovicidal activity comparable to albendazole, in addition to inducing morphological alterations in the eggs (Carvalho et al. 2020). In a study evaluating sixteen essential oils from S. guianensis, activity was observed against the promastigote forms of Leishmania (L.) amazonensis (Andrade et al. 2016). The essential oil from S. guianensis leaves, composed of b-myrcene, germacrene D, and bicyclogermacrene, was the most effective in inhibiting protozoan growth; however, it exhibited higher cytotoxicity toward L6 and L cells compared with the other samples (Andrade et al. 2016). Overall, extracts, essential oils, and fractions of S. guianensis display inhibitory activity against parasites such as ticks, helminths, and protozoa, indicating potential for the treatment of related diseases. Antitumoral activity Traditionally known in the Amazon region as ‘‘capitiu´,’’ the species S. guianensis exhibits high variability in the chemotypes of its essential oils. Recent chemical studies have identiﬁed curzerenone (16.4%), drimenol (13.7%), and spathulenol (12.4%) as major constituents of the essential oil of this plant collected in Brazil. Curzerenone has been associated in bioactivity studies with potential cytotoxic effects in tumor cell models, including the ability to induce apoptosis in cancer cell lines, suggesting a possible antitumor role for its derivatives. Furthermore, spathulenol is frequently linked to immune system modulation and demonstrates antiproliferative properties in different biological systems, reinforcing the pharmacological interest in oxygenated sesquiterpenes present in the essential oil of S. guianensis. According to Barbosa et al. (2023), this proﬁle had not been previously described in the literature, strengthening the inﬂuence of edaphoclimatic, seasonal, and geographic factors on the synthesis of secondary metabolites. This ﬁnding contributes to expanding the phytochemical knowledge of the species and highlights the importance of 123 5440 Phytochem Rev (2026) 25:5405–5446

regional studies with Amazonian medicinal species (Martins et al. 2021). Barbosa et al. (2023) conducted a study that integrates chemical analyses (GFID and GC-MS), in vitro antioxidant assays (DPPH and b-carotene/ linoleic acid) and in vivo evaluation based on the experimental oncology model with the Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC) model to test the efﬁcacy of S. guianensis essential oil. In this context, in vivo tests showed that after administration of 100 mg/kg of the oil, it not only reduced the volume of ascitic ﬂuid but also preserved the viability of hepatocytes, suggesting low systemic toxicity compared to conventional chemotherapeutic agents. Decreases in malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity in liver tissues indicated a protective effect against tumor-induced oxidative stress. These results are consistent with the literature that associates the control of oxidative stress with the inhibition of tumor progression (Marnett 1999). The antitumor effect of S. guianensis essential oil can be deﬁned by its complex composition of sesquiterpenes, which has a synergistic effect that inhibits and protects the body against oxidative damage. In silico analyses In silico studies on S. guianensis have provided signiﬁcant insights into the potential molecular mechanisms underlying experimentally observed biological activities. These computational approaches have been primarily applied to establish correlations between the major sesquiterpenes present in the essential oil and relevant biological targets, employing methodologies such as homology modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and binding energy calculations. Such strategies enable the rationalization of bioactivity at the molecular level and support the identiﬁcation of key ligand–target interactions (Toledo et al. 2019; Santana de Oliveira et al. 2020; Martins et al. 2021; Costa et al. 2022; Montan˜oCampaz et al. 2025). Research by Toledo et al. (2019) regarding insecticides and selectivity offered the use of computational modeling speciﬁcally with b-myrcene and 2-undecanone, hypothesizing that the main constituents of the essential oil of S. guianensis act as TRP (Transient Receptor Potential) channels of Myzus persicae. Therefore, homology modeling (Swiss-Model) integrated with molecular docking (Autodock 4) was employed in the study. The main results highlight that both compounds bound to the TRP channel, speciﬁcally the lipid activation site where 2-undecanone formed an immunity bond with Ser450 and hydrophobic van der Waals interactions with residues Y470, L451, M467, D446, S448, and T449, showing a modulating ligand proﬁle. b-Myrcene exhibited exclusively hydrophobic interactions with alkyl/p-alkyl type contacts with Y470, L451, M467, high compatibility with the lipid environment of the channel, which is consistent with the nonpolar nature of the compound (Adams 2007). Finally, when evaluating selectivity via docking, it was observed that no stable interaction was noted between the compounds and the TRP channel of the predictions. Further investigations using in silico studies were employed to support the larvicidal mechanism of action of Siparuna essential oils against Aedes aegypti, aiming to verify which essential mosquito proteins could be molecularly affected by the sesquiterpenes celemene and germacrene D (Montan˜o-Campaz et al. 2025). Thus, homology modeling of AChE was performed in the Swiss-Model, where high structural identity and model validation were veriﬁed with a Ramachandran of 93% of residues in favorable regions and a QMEAN factor of - 1.04, demonstrating that the enzyme structure is robust for docking. The data suggest that sesquiterpenes do not act as classic covalent inhibitors and likely exert non-competitive or mixed inhibition, in addition to interfering with the enzyme’s conformational dynamics, leading to acetylcholine accumulation and, conversely, neurotransmission dysregulation, resulting in larval paralysis and death. The study demonstrated that the ligands exhibited van der Waals interactions with important amino acid residues, with germacrene D showing an alkylhydrophobic interaction afﬁnity with Phe587 and celemene showing a p-alkyl interaction afﬁnity with Phe587 and Phe591 (Ramachandran and Sasisekharan 1968; Trott and Olson 2010; Waterhouse et al. 2018). Within the scope of prospecting for compounds with antimicrobial potential, an important study in this section focuses its analyses on molecular docking and molecular dynamics studies, in relation to metabolites such as atractylone, germacrene D and c-elemene, which showed signiﬁcant afﬁnity for essential molecular targets, including insect acetylcholinesterase 123 Phytochem Rev (2026) 25:5405–5446 5441

(AChE) and key enzymes involved in microbial metabolism (Andrade et al. 2013; Nelita et al. 2015). Molecular docking analyses revealed the predominance of stable hydrophobic interactions at the active site of the target proteins, as well as the punctual occurrence of hydrogen bonds with conserved catalytic residues. These results allowed the ranking of the compounds and the selection of the most promising complexes for the molecular dynamics stage. MD simulations demonstrated that the most active molecules form stable complexes with the target protein, exhibiting convergent RMSD and good ligand ﬁt, while RMSF showed reduced ﬂexibility of the active site residues and maintenance of the main intermolecular interactions over time. Free energy calculations by MM-PBSA conﬁrmed favorable binding afﬁnities, with a predominant contribution from hydrophobic interactions, corroborating the proposed antimicrobial mechanism. These interaction patterns suggest plausible mechanisms of enzymatic inhibition, corroborating the effects observed in in vitro and in vivo biological assays previously described in the literature (Melo et al. 2017; Santana de Oliveira et al. 2020). In the neurobiological ﬁeld, Martins et al. (Martins et al. 2021) conducted computational screenings targeting acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition, which indicated that oxygenated sesquiterpenes, especially shyobunone and iso-shyobunone, showed satisfactory steric complementarity with the binding site and peripheral regions of the enzyme, with the latter being the strongest ligand as it presented the best binding energy (-8.0 kcal/mol). Docking of the two binding sites revealed two preferential pockets in the AChE catalytic channel. The innermost region, A, involves residues Trp108, Tyr146, Gly143-148, Try155, Phe315, Tyr355, and His494. This region proved to be the closest, but not coincident with, the classic catalytic triad (Ser-His-Glu). The outermost region, site B, peripheral to the enzyme, involves residues such as Tyr94, Trp304, Phe313-315, Tyr355, and Tyr359, which is associated with allosteric modulation of AChE. These ﬁndings support the hypothesis of a possible non-competitive inhibition mechanism, previously suggested by kinetic and spectroscopic analyses, and also showed dominant hydrophobic interactions and some stabilizing hydrogen bonds (Valentini et al. 2010; Andrade et al. 2015). Conclusions This integrated scientometric, chemometric, and pharmacological analysis demonstrates that Siparuna guianensis essential oil is a chemically polymorphic natural product whose biological performance is strongly chemotype-dependent. Current evidence supports consistent bioactivity in insecticidal, antiparasitic, antimicrobial, enzyme-inhibitory, and antitumoral models, yet the ﬁeld remains largely driven by chemical proﬁling and preliminary screening assays. Mechanistic pharmacology, dose, response characterization, and translational validation are still limited. Future research should prioritize chemotype standardization linked to botanical origin, plant organ, and extraction parameters to improve reproducibility across studies. Mechanism-oriented investigations using molecular, cellular, and systems pharmacology approaches are needed to conﬁrm proposed targets such as acetylcholinesterase, membrane integrity pathways, and replication enzymes. Comparative testing of isolated major constituents versus wholeoil matrices should be expanded to clarify synergistic and antagonistic interactions. In vivo pharmacokinetics, toxicology, and selectivity studies in mammalian models represent a critical gap that must be addressed before therapeutic consideration. Advanced delivery systems, including nanoformulations and encapsulation platforms, show promise for enhancing stability, bioavailability, and safety and should be systematically optimized. Finally, multicenter collaborative studies integrating metabolomics, chemometrics, and pharmacodynamics are recommended to establish predictive chemotype-activity models and accelerate the rational pharmacological development of S. guianensis essential oil. Chemical Composition and Anti-Candida and Anti- Trypanosoma cruzi Activities of Essential Oils from the Rhizomes and Leaves of Brazilian Species of Renealmia L. fil.

Kathlyn V. Gevú 1, Helena R.P. Lima 2*, Ilzenayde A. Neves 3, Érica O. Mello 4, Gabriel B. Taveira 4, Laís P. Carvalho 1, Mário G. Carvalho 3, Valdirene M. Gomes 4, Edésio J.T. Melo 1 and Maura Da Cunha 1

1Laboratório de Biologia Celular e Tecidual, Centro de Biociências e Biotecnologia, Universidade Estadual do Norte Fluminense Darcy Ribeiro, Campos dos Goytacazes, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 2Laboratório de Anatomia Vegetal, Departamento de Botânica, Instituto de Ciências Biológicas e da Saúde, Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro, Seropédica, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 3Laboratório de Química de Produtos Naturais, Departamento de Química, Instituto de Ciências Exatas, Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro, Seropédica, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 4Laboratório de Fisiologia e Bioquímica de Microrganismos, Centro de Biociências e Biotecnologia, Universidade Estadual do Norte Fluminense Darcy Ribeiro, Campos dos Goytacazes, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (Received August 04, 2018; Revised October 16, 2018; Accepted October 17, 2018)

Abstract: This work aimed to determine the chemical composition of essential oils from rhizomes and leaves of Renealmia chrysotricha Petersen, R. breviscapa Poepp. & Endl. and R. nicolaioides Loes., and to evaluate the biological activities of these oils on three Candida species and the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. The rhizomes and leaves were collected in the Atlantic and Amazon rainforests. Essential oils were isolated and characterized by gas chromatography. Βeta-Caryophyllene was found to be the most predominant compound in the essential oils of rhizomes and leaves of R. breviscapa, and the rhizomes of R. nicolaioides, whereas (E)-nerolidol was the most abundant compound in the oils of leaves of R. nicolaioides. In R. chrysotricha, α-terpineol, coronarin-E and 1,8-cineole were found to be the most predominant compounds in the essential oils of rhizomes, whereas cis-3hexenol was predominant in the leaves. The tested oils did not inhibit C. albicans growth at 1000 µg/mL, whereas leaf oils from R. chrysotricha and R. nicolaioides inhibited the growth of C. buinensis and C. tropicalis by about 50%. Essential oils from the rhizomes and leaves of R. chrysotricha exhibited efficient antiparasitic activity against Trypanosoma cruzi. Damage to T. cruzi epimastigotes was confirmed by LM and TEM.

Keywords: Zingiberaceae; rhizomes; leaves; terpenoids; anticandidal activity; antiparasitic activity. © 2019 ACG Publications. All rights reserved.

1. Introduction Fungal and protozoan diseases are widely disseminated and very common among tropical countries. These diseases are difficult to treat because the pathogens can develop resistance to

269 medications or because of side effects of treatments [1], and so natural products derived from plants have been used as a source of replacement drugs [2]. Plants of the family Zingiberaceae are well known for producing essential oils (EOs) that are used to prevent and control several diseases, according to descriptive and biological studies [3-9]. The activity of essential oils from the rhizomes of nine species of Zingiberaceae (Zingiber officinale Rosc., Z. cassumunar Roxb., Z. zerumbet Smith, Curcuma aeruginosa Roxb., C. mangga Valeton and van Zyp, C. xanthorrhiza Roxb., Kaempferia galanga Linn., Alpinia galanga Swartz and Boesenbergia pandurata (Roxb.) Schlecht) against five dermatophytic fungi, three filamentous fungi and five yeast strains, including Candida albicans and C. tropicalis, obtained from the Institute for Medical Research Kuala Lumpur, was evaluated [3]. The essential oils from Zingiber officinale and Z. cassumunar showed the greatest activity against species of Candida, forming an inhibition zone of 11.7-15.7 mm. The rhizome essential oil of Zingiber nimmonii was found to inhibit the fungi Candida glabrata, C. albicans and Aspergillus niger, with the inhibition zones reaching 9-12 mm in diameter [4]. The essential oils from different parts (leaf blade, leaf sheath and rhizome) of Aframomum sceptrum (Oliv. & T. Hanb) K. Schum. did not inhibit the growth of C. albicans [5], whereas rhizome oil of Curcuma longa L. exhibited moderate activity (MIC = 0.625 g/mL) against 11 Candida albicans strains and one C. glabrata strain isolated from human clinical material [6]. The antifungal and antiparasitic activity of rhizome essential oil from Aframomum spectrum (Oliv. and D. Hanb) K. Schum., as well as that of its major compounds (β-pinene and caryophyllene oxide) [7]. The authors concluded that the oil exhibited moderate activity against C. albicans, and high activity against Trypanosoma brucei brucei. The activity of rhizome and leaf essential oils from Hedychium coronarium J. König., as well as the activity of their major compounds against the procyclic Trypanosoma brucei. Caryophyllene oxide exhibited the greatest activity, with its lethal concentration for 50% of parasites varying between 24.53 and 65.77 g/mL for a variety of strains [8]. Renealmia L. fil. (Zingiberaceae) comprises 75 herbaceous and rhizomatous species from the Neotropical region and Africa [10]. A review by Negrelle [11] addressed botanical, ecological, pharmacological and agronomic aspects of the species of Renealmia, and emphasized that few of the species have had their chemical composition evaluated. In Brazil, this genus is represented by 21 species distributed in all phytogeographic domains and in all regions of the country, 14 of which are found in the Northern Region [12]. Recent studies with essential oil-producing species of the Amazon region have been performed with the purpose of evaluating biological activities, such as antimicrobial, antioxidant and cytotoxic behaviors [13,14]. A previous study by Luz et al. [15] elucidated the composition of leaf oil of R. floribunda K. Schum., and found β-pinene to be the predominant compound. For Renelamia alpinia (Rottb.) Maas, β-caryophyllene, allo-aromadendrene and β-pinene were detected in stems, leaves and fruits, respectively [16]. For leaves of R. thyrsoidea (Ruiz &Pav.), terpinolene and α-phellandrene were identified as major, and were found to exhibit antimicrobial activity against gram-negative bacteria, and antioxidant activity via the ABTS method [17]. The present work aimed to determine the composition of essential oils from leaves and rhizomes of Renealmia chrysotricha Petersen, R. breviscapa Poepp. & Endl. and R. nicolaioides Loes., and to evaluate the biological activities of these compounds on different yeasts and the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi.

2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Plant Materials

Rhizomes and leaves of R. chrysotricha were collected in the Parque Nacional de Itatiaia in May of 2015, while those for R. breviscapa and R. nicolaioides were collected at the Fazenda Experimental Catuaba (10°4′40"S×67°37′35"W)and in the Reserva Florestal Humaitá (9°45′17"S×67°40′15"W) located in Rio Branco, state of Acre, in June of 2015. The material was identified and deposited in the Herbarium of the Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro (RBR), voucher 33416 for R.

Chemical composition activities species of Renealmia essential oils

270 chrysotricha, and in the Herbarium of the Universidade Federal do Acre (UFACPZ), vouchers 6645 and 6646 for R. breviscapa and R. nicolaioides, respectively.

2.2 Extraction of Essential Oils

Fresh rhizomes (115 g ± 10) and leaves (420 g ± 20) of R. chrysotricha, R. breviscapa and R. nicolaioides were hydrodistilled using a modified Clevenger Extractor [18]. The extraction was carried out for 2 h. The obtained oil layers were separated and dried over anhydrous sodium sulphate, stored in hermetically sealed glass containers and kept under refrigeration at 4 °C before analysis. The yield of the essential oil was calculated and expressed as weight of oil per weight of fresh rhizomes. The oils obtained from rhizomes and leaves were analyzed by analytical gas chromatography (GC-FID) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). The GC-FID analyses were performed with a Hewlett-Packard 5890 SERIES II chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector and a fused silica capillary column (Factor Four-VF-5ms - 30 m x 0.25 mm i.d. x 0.25 mm film thickness). The analyses were performed first between the programmed temperatures of 60-260 °C (increments of 3 °C/min), and subsequently from 10°C/min to 290 °C, using helium as carrier gas at a flow rate of 1 mL/min, with an injector temperature of 220 °C, interface at 310 °C, detector temperature of 280 °C, and the injection of 1.0 μL of essential oil diluted in dichloromethane. The GC-MS analyses were carried out with a Shimadzu GC-EM, GC-17A/ QP2010 Plus, with ion source at 220 °C and electron ionization mode at 70 eV. The chromatographic conditions were identical to those described above. The analyses were performed at a scanning speed of 0.5 scan/s with a m/z 40–550 scanning layer. The relative amount (%) of each oil component was expressed as a percentage of signal area in relation to the total signal area of the oil. The components of the essential oils were characterized by comparing their spectra with a database, with literature records and by calculating the Kovat’s retention index [19-21].

2.3 Anti-Candida Activity

The yeasts Candida albicans (CE022), Candida buinensis (3982) and Candida tropicalis (CE017) were cultivated in Sabouraud medium [peptone 10 g/L, D-(+) glucose 20 g/L, agar-agar 17 g/L; Merck S/A], maintained at 23 °C and stored at the Laboratório de Fisiologia e Bioquímica de Microrganismos, in the Centro de Biociências e Biotecnologia, of the Universidade Estadual do Norte Fluminense Darcy Ribeiro (UENF), Campos dos Goytacazes, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Yeast cells (C. albicans, C. buinensis and C. tropicalis inoculates) were removed from the tubes containing Sabouraud agar and transferred to Petri dishes containing the same agar. The cells were maintained at 30 °C for two days. After this period, the cells were used in the assay by removing colonies with an inoculation loop, adding them to 10 mL of culture medium (Sabouraud broth) and quantifying them using a Neubauer chamber (same as used for quantifying fungal spores) under a Zeiss Axiovision 4 light microscope. After quantification, the cells of the yeasts C. albicans, C. buinensis and C. tropicalis (1 x 104 cells m/L) were incubated in 200 L of Sabouraud containing a stock solution of the essential oil samples was prepared in 10% DMSO at a concentration of 1000 g m/L of essential oil from rhizomes or leaves of R. chrysotricha, R. breviscapa or R. nicolaioides. The assay was performed in 96-well culture plates and incubated at 30 °C for 24 h. To observe inhibition of fungal growth, optical density was calculated from readings with a microplate reader (EZ Read 400, Biochrom), at 620 nm every 6 h. Negative controls without addition of essential oil samples were also determined. The entire assay was done in triplicate and under aseptic conditions in a laminar flow hood following an adaptation of the methodology of [22].

2.4 Antiparasitic Activity

Epimastigotes of Trypanosoma cruzi (DM28 strain) were cultivated in 5 mL of liver infusion tryptose (LIT) medium supplemented with 10% FCS (fetal bovine serum, Gibco) and 4% of hemin at 28 °C. Every five days, 1 mL of parasites, still at exponential population growth, were placed in a

Gevú et.al., Rec. Nat. Prod. (2019) 13:3 268-280

271 fresh tube, in which fresh culture medium was added to reach 5 mL. Much research has been performed using the epimastigote of T. cruzi because it is easily cultivated in vitro and, consequently, widely used in preliminary experimental studies. For cytotoxicity testing of R. chrysotricha essential oil on epimastigotes, different volumes of stock solution were incubated in a 96-well plate to give final concentrations of 25, 100, 400 and 800 µg/mL, with the final concentration of DMSO being less than 1.5% at all concentrations. In addition, 100 µL of parasites, at a density of 1.3 x 106 cells/mL, were added per well and the volume was adjusted to 200 µL using culture medium. The plate containing the experiment was incubated at 28 °C for 24 and 48 h. Negative controls without addition of essential oil samples were also determined. Quantification of parasites was done in a Neubauer chamber. For morphological analysis, epimastigotes of T. cruzi were centrifuged at 1700 rpm for 10 min, and washed with PBS (pH 7.2) at room temperature. The parasites were fixed in a solution of 4% paraformaldehyde diluted in PBS, and stained with Giemsa (10% v/v) for 2 h at room temperature. Aliquots of 100 µL were spread on microscope slides, dried at 37 °C and examined using a photoequipped Zeiss Axioplan light microscope. The images were obtained using the software Axiovision (ZEISS). For analysis of ultrastructure, the samples treated with 100 µg/mL of aqueous extract for 24 h were centrifuged for 10 min at 1700 RPM, washed with PBS for 10 more min and re-centrifuged at the same RPM. Fixation was performed using 4% formaldehyde, 1% glutaraldehyde, 0.2 M sodium cacodylate buffer, 1.5 mL distilled water and 5% sucrose for 1 h at room temperature. The samples were then centrifuged again for 10 min at 1700 RPM and washed with a 0.1 M solution of sodium cacodylate buffer. The resulting pellet was post-fixed with 2% osmium tetroxide and 0.8% potassium ferrocyanide for 1.5 h at ambient temperature and protected from light. The post-fixed samples were washed in sodium cacodylate buffer, centrifuged twice and dehydrated in an increasing series of acetone. After dehydration, the samples were incubated in a solution of 100% acetone-epon resin in proportions of 2:1, 1:1, 1:2 and pure epon resin, for 6 h each step. The material was then embedded in epon (Epoxy Resin) and polymerized in a kiln at 60 °C for 48 h. Ultrathin sections were obtained using an ultramicrotome (Reichert Ultracuts Leica Instruments®) and contrasted with 5% aqueous uranyl acetate for 20 min in the dark and lead citrate for 5 min. The material was observed and photographed with a Zeiss TEM 900 transmission electron microscope operating at an accelerating voltage of 80 kV.

3. Results and Discussion

3.1. Essential Oil Composition

The essential oil yields for R. chrysotricha, R. breviscapa and R. nicolaioides were 0.024%, 0.012% and 0.018% for rhizomes, and 0.0075%, 0.008% and 0.017% for the leaves, respectively. Tables 1 and 2 show the oil constituents. Nineteen constituents were identified in the rhizome essential oil of R. chrysotricha, which corresponded to 92.98% of all the oil, with the major constituents being α-terpineol, coronarin E and 1,8-cineole (Table 1). The monoterpene α-terpineol has been referred to as both antinociceptive [26] and bactericidal [27].The compound 1,8-cineole has been found to be profuse in rhizome essential oils of species of Zingiberaceae [8,28], and exhibits anti-inflammatory and antinociceptive activities [29]. The labdane diterpene coronarin E, also classified as a furanolabdanoid, was first isolated from the rhizome of Hedychium coronarium Roscoe [30], and later from H. gardnerianum Roscoe, H. ellipticum Buch.-Ham. ex Sm., H. longicornutum Bak., and H. spicatum [31-34]. This compound was also isolated from other genera of the same family, including Aframomum, Alpinia, Amomum and Curcuma [34-37]. This diterpene exhibited moderate activity against Mycobacterim tuberculosis, as well as cytotoxic activity [32,33].

Twelve and 26 components were detected in the rhizome essential oils of R. breviscapa and R. nicolaioides, respectively, with β-caryophyllene being the major constituent of both (Table 1). Among the 20 components identified in the essential oil of leaves of R. chrysotricha, cis-3hexenol was the most prominent compound (Table 2). In the leaves of R. breviscapa, 23 compounds were identified, with β-caryophyllene being the major constituent, as was also found for R. alpinia [16]. The essential oil of R. nicolaioides revealed 42 constituents, with (E)-nerolidol being predominant (Table 2). Studies have shown that the sesquiterpene (E)-nerolidol causes bacteria to be more susceptible to antibiotics [36] and inhibits growth of species of Leishmania [39]. The major constituents of the leaf oils of the studied species differed from those previously reported for R. alpinia, R. floribunda and R. thyrsoidea [15-17].

3.2. Anti-Candida Activity

The antimicrobial activities of the essential oils studied in this work were evaluated by exposing the yeasts C. albicans, C. buinensis and C. tropicalis to 1000 µg/mL essential oil, as shown in Figure 1. The results show that all tested oils, whether from rhizomes or leaves, failed to inhibit the growth of C. albicans cells (Figure 1A). A similar result was found for essential oils from the rhizome, leaf blade and leaf sheath of Aframomum spectrum [5]. The oil from leaves of R. chrysotricha exhibited greater activity, inhibiting 56% of the growth of C. buinensis at 1000 µg/mL (Figure 1B), whereas leaf oil from R. nicolaioides exhibited an effect on C. tropicalis, also at 1000 µg/mL (Figure 1C). Similar results were reported for essential oil from the rhizome of Curcuma longa L. (Zingiberaceae) against C. tropicalis [6]. Oxygenated compounds were the major constituents of essential oils from leaves (91,3% and 59.7%, respectively) and rhizomes (96.15% and 62.2%, respectively), of R. chrysotricha and R. nicolaioides, whereas in R. breviscapa hydrogenated compounds were found in greater amounts in rhizomes (80.33%), and in the same proportion of oxygenated compounds in leaves (48.17%).Some studies have shown that oxygenated compounds exhibit higher antimicrobial activity than hydrogenated compounds because of their ability to promote the formation of hydrogen bonds and the solubility of the oil in water [40,41], which corroborate our results.

3.3. Antiparasitic Activity

The essential oil from the rhizome of R. chrysotricha, at 25 µg/mL, reduced the number of parasites by 50% and 61%, after 24 and 48 h, respectively. Treatment with 100 µg/mL reduced the population of parasites by 56% after 24 h, with all parasites being eliminated within 48 h (Figure 2A). The leaf essential oil of R. chrysotricha was found to reduce the population of parasites by 2859% in concentrations of 25, 100, 400 and 800 µg/mL, after 24 h; and by 26-53% in concentrations of 25, 100 and 400 µg/mL, with total death of the parasites at 800 µg/mL, after 48 h (Figure 2B).

Our results using essential oils clearly show their potential lethality and ability to alter the morphology of T. cruzi epimastigotes. Both light and transmission electron microscopy revealed that untreated epimastigotes had a typical elongate shape, one flagellum and no visible alterations (Figure 3A and 4A). However, in the presence of essential oils from leaves (100 µg/mL) and rhizomes (25 µg/mL) for 48 h, the epimastigotes exhibited a rounded body, changes to flagellum morphology (Figure 3B and 3C), cytoplasmic vacuolization and mitochondrial swelling (Fig. 4B and 4C).

The remarkable anti-Trypanosoma cruzi activity of the essential oil from the rhizome of R. chrysotricha may be related to the presence of the labdane diterpenoid coronarin E, as one of the major components of that oil. Some studies have demonstrated potent activity by labdane diterpenoids against T. cruzi [42,43]. Changes to the morphology of species of Trypanosoma have been reported in other works after incubation of the parasite, whether in the presence of essential oil from species of Lamiaceae and Fabaceae [44,45]. Changes in ultrastructure were observed when the control was compared to treatments, similar to the results reported by Menna-Barreto et al. [45], suggesting that T. cruzi was undergoing an autophagic pathway [46]. In the present study, the oils tested against T. cruzi epimastigotes decreased the amount of parasites by 50% at 25 µg/mL, as reported for essential oils from Hedychium coronarium J. Koenig (Zingiberaceae) against the procyclic form of Trypanosoma brucei [8]. Essential oils from leaves were found to contain more substances than rhizome oils, probably due to the greater exposure of leaves to seasonal and climatic variation. The yield, recovery and quality of essential oil are influenced by photosynthesis, photoperiodic modulation, seasonal and climate variation, nutritional relationships, plant growth regulators and some abiotic stresses (light, moisture, salinity and temperature) [47,48]. Essential oils are composed of a variety of different compounds, with terpenes being the most representative. Antifungal and antiparasitic activities shown by some of the evaluated oils may be due to either synergism between their components or the action of predominant compounds. The most significant results against the Candida species studied were for the essential oil of R. chrysotricha leaves against C. buinenses, and for R. nicolaioides leaf oil against C. tropicalis. The significant activity of the rhizome oil of R. chrysotricha against T. cruzi suggests that the plant is a potential new source of agents to help the control of trypanosomiasis.

Antinociceptive Activity of Essential Oils from Wild Growing and Micropropagated Plants of Renealmia alpinia (Rottb.) Maas

Isabel Gómez-Betancur 1*, Dora Benjumea 1, Juan E. Gómez 1, Natalia Mejía 1 and Juan F. León 2

1 Programa Ofidismo-Escorpionismo, Facultad de Ciencias Farmacéuticas y Alimentarias, Universidad de Antioquia, Medellín 1226, Colombia 2 Department of Medicinal Chemistry, College of Pharmacy, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, 32610, United States

(Received January 26, 2018; Revised April 11, 2018; Accepted April 12, 2018)

Abstract: Renealmia alpinia is a medicinal plant that has been cultivated and used for the treatment of headaches, abdominal pain, as a febrifuge and to treat snake bites in southeast Colombia and in the Caribbean islands. Moreover, its edible fruits are commonly used as spice in Mexico. The R. alpinia leave-extracts have shown enzymatic inhibition of Bothrops atrox and Bothrops asper snake poison. The extracts also showed effects as a peripheral analgesic agent. This report investigates the analgesic activity of the essential oils obtained by hydrodistillation from wild and in vitro propagation samples of R. alpinia as well as the chemical profile using GC-MS. The essential oils isolated from R. alpinia evaluated on concentrations of 50, 75 and 100 mg/kg showed significant antinociceptive effects in the test of acetic-acid-induced abdominal writhing, compared to the control animals. The essential oil of the wild flora leaves showed the highest percentage of pain inhibition by 200 mg/kg, concluding that the essential oil of R. alpinia presents antinociceptive activity in an in vivo model. These results help us to understand the traditional use of R. alpinia to treat pain and make it a potential source for the development of phytopharmaceutics. .

Keywords: Renealmia alpinia; essential oil; antinociceptive; micropropagation . © 2018 ACG Publications. All rights reserved.

1. Introduction Pain is one of the health problems that most affects the quality of people’s lives, which produces a significant economic and social burden [1]. According to the Colombian Association for the study of Pain, 70% of the Colombian population has suffered some sort of pain during the last six months (acute and chronic), 47% for chronic pain (64.5% of musculoskeletal type - in lower limbs and back, 23% of craniofacial type, and 7.8% of abdominal pain) and between severe and moderate intensity (41.0% and 39.0%, respectively) [2]. Phytotherapy is an important alternative for the treatment of pain because it is accessible to wide range of the population, covering the needs of primary care in health [3,4] in developing countries and also in developed countries such as Italy,

11 Germany and France, as an alternative or complementary therapy [3,5]. The motivations for the use of medicinal plants as therapy for the treatment of pain result from disappointment with conventional therapies, due in many cases to their lack of effectiveness, as well as fear of the adverse/side effects of the drugs especially non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) [6,7]. Some extracts and essential oils from plants of the Zingiberaceae family have shown to be active in the treatment of pain [8-10]. This is particularly prevalent in southeast Colombia where indigenous natives use R. alpinia in the treatment of bites by poisonous snakes [11]. This plant has also been used in other countries in the Americas for the treatment of headache [12] and stomach pain [13], among others maladies. Moreover, the fruits and leaves of R. alpinia play an important role as a spice in some regions of Mexico. In fact, the aril of the fruits is used to enhance flavor in tortillas, and their leaves are used as wrapping for different kinds of food [14,15]. Our studies have shown that rhizomes and leaf extracts of R. alpinia inhibit the toxic and lethal effects of the poisonous venom of the Bothrops atrox and B. asper [16-18]. We also found that the main bioactive component of the dichloromethane extract is the flavanone pinostrobin that has the inhibitory capacity of the coagulant, proteolytic, hemolytic and hemorrhagic effects of B. atrox- B. asper poison [18]. Moreover, some isolated R. alpinia pure compounds were evaluated through the Siegmund test to assess activity on the peripheral nervous system [18] in animal models. The objective of this research is the evaluation of the analgesic activity of two R. alpinia essential oils obtained from leaves of wild and micropropagated plant samples. In addition, a comparative chemical analysis of the essential oils was carried out by gas-chromatography massspectroscopy (GC-MS).

2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Plant Material The leaves of R. alpinia (Rottb.) Maas obtained from wild flora were collected in Dantas village, located in the municipality of San Rafael, latitude 06° 118' N 75° 101' W (Antioquia-Colombia). It was identified and authenticated at the Herbarium of the University of Antioquia (HUA) and assigned a voucher number 176395. In vitro culture of R. alpinia was obtained from three hundred and sixty (360) seedlings collected in the village of Titumate, Unguía, (5 m.a.s.l, Chocó, Colombia). It germinated in a room at the biological station of the University of Antioquia, and was identified in the HUA. The seedlings were washed once with iodine soap and running water, disinfected through exposure to sodium hypochlorite (NaClO) (2 %, 25 min), then transferred aseptically to culture vials with a nutrient medium previously sterilized by moist heat (121 °C). The environment is made up of basic salts of Murashige and Skoog [19,20], pH = 5.8, sucrose (30 g/L) and agar (7 g/L). Once established, the micropropagated seedlings were subjected to subculture every four weeks, kept at a controlled temperature (25 °C) and photoperiod of 1 day (16 h of light, 50 mol m- 2 s- 1). Both the wild plant material and micropropagated plants were dried at 38° C for 4 h and then pulverized in a mill (Covenant Electro motor RPM 50 Hz) after which they were deposited and stored in airtight containers in a cool, dry place and protected until usage.

2.2. Extraction of Essential Oils To obtain the essential oils of wild R. alpinia (EORaw) and in vitro culture (EORaiv), the following methodology was carried out: the plant materials underwent hydrodistillation in a Clevenger-type device, with recirculation, refrigerated water and temperature control until depleting extraction (2 h, boiling temperature); 180 g of wild plant material and 90 g of plant material of culture in vitro were used, obtaining yields of 0.07 % and 0.04 % respectively; the collected essential oils were dried by adding sodium anhydrous sulfate, packed in glass bottles and stored under refrigeration (4 °C); the vials were protected from light and humidity until usage.

2.3. Experimental Animals Swiss mice (males and females) with a weight of 23 ± 1 g were used, supplied by the animal facility of the University of Antioquia. The animals were previously housed at room temperature (22 ± 1 °C) relative humidity of 50-60 % and 12 h of light-dark cycles with food and free access to water. Two days prior to the experiment, the mice were allowed to adapt to the environment. The animals were treated under the standards of care for experimental animals of the Canadian Council for the Protection of Animals, with the endorsement of the Ethics Committee for the Experimentation with Animals of the University of Antioquia, Act No. 65/2010, and in accordance with law 84 of 1989 of the Congress of Colombia.

2.4. Analgesic Activity In order to evaluate the analgesic activity, the following method was developed [21]: mice were randomly separated into seven groups (4 animals per group), then administered orally with the negative control group receiving vehicle (Tween 80, 5%) and the positive control group receiving ibuprofen 75 mg/kg (PBS, pH 7.2 buffer solution). The five remaining groups received doses of essential oil of wild and in vitro culture R. alpinia, of 50, 100 and 200 mg/kg for EORaw, and 50 and 100 mg/kg for EORaiv. After 30 minutes, all of the mice received an intraperitoneal injection of phenylquinone (4 mg/kg). 5 min later, the mice were placed in individual boxes for observation and the number of back-abdominal stretches were determined as evidence of visceral pain for a period of 15 min. Mice with a decrease in the number of twists were protected by the respective dose of essential oil. The percentage of inhibition of pain was calculated by the formula: % I= Gc – Gt/Gc * 100 Where Gc is the average of the negative control group stretches and Gt is an average of stretches of the treated group.

2.5. Statistical Analysis The results were expressed as the values of the mean ± SEM of measurements in each group. A comparison of the groups was performed using an analysis of variance (ANOVA) one-way with Dunnett’s test post hoc. A p-value p<0,05 criterion of statistical significance was applied. The GraphPad Prism® software for statistical analysis was used.

2.6. GC/MS Analysis The chemical analysis of the essential oils was performed by gas chromatography-mass spectrophotometry (GC–MS) on a Varian gas chromatograph 3800® coupled with mass spectrometer Varian Saturn ion trap 2000®. The electron impact ionization technique (70 eV) and selected mass range 40-350 m/z were used. Carrier gas was helium at rate of 1 mL/min. The samples were run in two different columns: 1. Capillary column Carbowax 20M® (30 m x 0.25 mm i.d. x 0,25 μm film), program of temperature: 45°C for 3 min, 45 - 240°C to 5 °C/min, temperature of the injector 230 °C, mode of injection 1 μL to split (1:15). 2. Capillary column DB - 5ms® (50 m x 0.20 mm i.d.x 0.33 μm film), program of temperature: 45 ° C for 3 min, 45 - 280 °C to 5 °C/min, 280 °C for 15 min, temperature of the injector 240 °C, mode of injection 1 μL to split (1:15). Identification of the components was made by comparing their mass spectra with those stored in the libraries of AMDIS/NIST®, and taking as reference the chemical characterization of essential oil of R. alpinia by Maia et al [22].

3. Results and Discussion

3.1 Analgesic activity

Mice treated with EORaw and EORaiv in doses of 50, 100, 200 mg/kg, and 50 and 100 mg/kg respectively, experienced a significant reduction in stretching, compared with the negative control group, with higher doses having greater effect. The highest percentage of inhibition of pain presented itself in the EORaw 200 mg/kg (92.0%). Table 1 revealed that the essential oils obtained from wild flora are more potent than the in vitro cultured. For example, with a 100 mg/kg dose, the essential oil sample from wild flora showed an inhibition percentage of 88.5 %, greater than the essential oil of cultivation in vitro, which was 79.2 %, with comparable data of the positive control ibuprofen at 75 mg/kg dose 84.0 %. We showed that oral administration of both essential oils of R. alpinia wild and micropropagated at doses of 50, 100 and 200 mg/kg produced significant dose-dependent inhibition against the chemical induced nociception test model (Table 1). Terpenes, the main constituents of R. alpinia essential oils showed interesting results that confirm its analgesic and anti-inflammatory activity [23]. Fonseca et al, showed that nerolidol has effects in chemical nociception models and demonstrated that the analgesic activity is mediated by the peripheral nervous system and not by the central nervous system, conducting experiments for both cases and that activity is related to the GABAergic system [24]. In addition, according to Chavan [25], the caryophyllene oxide, which is the second most important component in EORaiv, possesses some antinociceptive properties that have demonstrated centrally and peripherally mediated analgesia by caryophyllene oxide. Based on the above, it is possible to suggest that the higher percentage of trans-Nerolidol and caryophyllene/caryophyllene oxide can be considered as responsible for the antinociceptive activity of R. alpinia essential oils. Phenylquinone induced writhing test in mice is used to screen and study compounds for peripherally mediated analgesic activity. Peritoneal administration of phenylquinone induces endogenous pain mediators such as prostaglandins, histamine, serotonin (5-HT) and bradykinin that sensitize pain nerve endings. The released prostaglandins, mainly prostacyclin (PGI2) and to lesser extent PGE2 and PGF2α have been held responsible for pain sensation. Our results highlight the important role of analgesic activity with a mechanism of action that could be similar to ibuprofen, which prevents the synthesis of prostaglandins through inhibition of the enzyme cyclooxygenase 1 and 2 (COX1, COX2). Consequently, this brings about a decrease in the formation of precursors of prostaglandins and thromboxanes, resulting in an obvious pain decrease. We suggest that the R. alpinia essential oils carry a significant peripherally mediated analgesic [26,27].

Essential oils are a group of secondary metabolites that currently have a productive significance [31]. Many of them are valued for their qualities as potential medicinal products [32] and cosmetics [33]. In this study, the use of two chromatographic columns was fundamental, one with polar characteristics (Carbowax 20M®), and the other with apolar characteristics (DB - 5ms®), since they complemented the research well, generating confidence in the results obtained. A hydrodistillation method was employed for the extraction of volatiles from vegetal material (micropropagated and wild), using short times (90-180 m), controlled temperature (water recirculation at 4 ºC) and scarce loss of compounds that grant product aroma and biofunctionality.

15 Table 2 shows that the essential oil of wild samples contains greater wealth from the chemical point of view than the essential oil of in vitro culture revealing substantial differences in the chemical composition. Although, the main component in both essential oils is trans-nerolidol, its percentage in EORaw (40.9 %) is almost 9 % more than in the oil of the micropropagated plant (32 %) (Table 2). In addition, the second main component found in wild R. alpinia is the α-pinene (31.4 %) while in the micropropagated plant this compound only represents 1 %. On the other hand, for the micropropagated plant, we identified caryophyllene oxide as the second most abundant component (15.9 %), while in the wild plant this compound only represents 2.5 % of its composition. In general, the analysis of the R. alpinia essential oils derived from the identification of sixteen compounds. Four of them were not reported before for this botanical species (dihydroedulan II, β-elemene, farnesyl methyl ester and valencene). Our results are in accordance with previous reports for Renealmia genus essential oils, where terpenes are the main components [34, 35]. The difference in the composition can be attributed to the development conditions of the plants. Abiotic factors such as humidity, temperature, pH and soil nutrients create environmental stress on the plant and this is likely to result in production of additional secondary metabolites. Besides, the plants exposed to abiotic stimulus with which they have coevolved, also promote the development of different biosynthetic pathways through which a large variety of secondary metabolites are biosynthesized [36, 37]. In summary, our results contribute to the knowledge on the use of this medicinal plant. The findings demonstrate that the essential oil of R. alpinia presents analgesic activity with significant results on an in vivo model. This is the first time that the R. alpinia essential oils were studied in relation to their in vivo antinociceptive activity. Future studies are underway to identify its mechanism of analgesic action. These results suggested the potential feasibility of R. alpinia as a food ingredient, as well as their possible applications in the pharmaceutical industry.

Phenolic compounds from the rhizome of Renealmia nicolaioides Loes.: a new diarylheptanoid. An Acad Bras Cienc 91: e20180312. DOI 10.1590/0001-3765201920180312. Abstract: This study aims to identify phenolic compounds in dichloromethane and methanolic extracts of the rhizome of Renealmia nicolaioides collected in the North Region of Brazil. Two known diarylheptanoids, 1,7-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)-(1E)-1-hepten-3-one (1), and 5R-1,7-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)- 1E-hepten-5-ol (2), and a new one (1R,2S,5S)-2-hydroxy-1,7(p-hydroxyphenyl)-centrolobine (3), as well as one flavonoid, 3-metoxi-quercetin (4) were isolated by chromatographic procedure and identified by spectroscopic techniques (1H and13C NMR, HRMS and CD). The acetyl derivative of 2 was used to confirm its structure. All four compounds are reported for the first time for this genus, and this is the first occurrence of compound 1 as a natural metabolite. The results reported here are unprecedented for the genus Renealmia. Key words: Flavonoid, Alpinieae tribe, Zingiberaceae, underground organ. Correspondence to: Maura da Cunha E-mail: maurauenf@gmail.com ORCid: http://orcid.org/0000-0003-1078-3742 INTRODUCTION The genus Renealmia L.f. belongs to the family Zingiberaceae, subfamily Alpinioideae, and tribe Alpinieae, and contains approximately 75 species distributed throughout tropical regions of the Americas and Africa (Maas 1977). In Brazil, the genus is represented by 21 species distributed throughout several regions and phytogeographical domains of the country including Amazonia, Caatinga, Cerrado, Atlantic Forest, Pampa, and the Pantanal (Maas and Maas 2015). Some species of Renealmia are used for medicinal purposes, with anticancer activity and snakebite treatment being the most notable (Negrelle 2015). Phytochemical investigations have been conducted with species of Renealmia and have revealed the presence of terpenes, flavonoids and diarylheptanoids (Luz et al. 1984, Ramiandrasoa et al. 1986, Lognay et al. 1991, Zhou et al. 1997, Yang et al. 1999, Kaplan et al. 2000, Sekiguchi et al. 2001, 2002, Gu et al. 2002, Maia et al. 2007,
